title: Results For Every Competition At The AAU Junior Olympic Games
description: A results page for every competition at the 2026 AAU Junior Olympic Games Track And Field live on FloTrack.
fullText:
The final day of the 2026 AAU Junior Olympics is here, and the nation's top youth track and field athletes continued to shine at Drake Stadium in Des Moines, Iowa.

Throughout the week, athletes have battled through preliminary rounds and event finals while chasing AAU Junior Olympic titles and national records.

World Record! Asher Denman Breaks Boys 9-Year-Old Long Jump Mark At AAU Junior Olympics

Updated Wanda Diamond League Standings

Several meet records have already fallen, highlighting the depth of talent on display as competitors continue to make their mark on one of the country's premier youth track and field stages.

Stay up to date with every result from the 2026 AAU Junior Olympics and don't miss a second of action from Drake University throughout the week.

title: Giants 3B Matt Chapman likely to undergo season-ending surgery for hernia, core muscle tear
description: Chapman has been on the injured list since July 1 and is scheduled to visit a specialist in Philadelphia before expected surgery.
fullText:
San Francisco Giants third baseman Matt Chapman is expected to undergo season-ending surgery to repair a hernia and core muscle tear, according to reports.

Chapman, 33, will see specialist Dr. William Meyers in Philadelphia on Sunday, the San Francisco Chronicle's Susan Slusser reported. The 10-year veteran will then likely have surgery on Tuesday.

"He's going to go see an expert in that field and be sure about what needs to be done," Giants manager Tony Vitello told reporters on Friday, via MLB.com. "Surgery's probably more likely than not."

"But I think getting squared away with that doctor and [being] 100% about what's the best path," he added. "If that is the path, it would be the end of his season on the field.

The Giants are 49-67 going into Saturday's play, placing them fourth in the NL West, 20 games behind the Los Angeles Dodgers.

Chapman has struggled with the injury throughout the season. He has been on the injured list since July 1 with what was termed an "abdominal strain." The third baseman was noticeably uncomfortable during the Giants' 8-2 loss to the Arizona Diamondbacks on June 30.

In the sixth inning, Chapman fielded a chopper and threw out catcher Gabriel Moreno but was limping and favoring the top of his right leg as he came off the field. Chapman batted in the seventh and hit an infield pop-out, but limped to first base and subsequently left the game.

Chapman's 2026 season will end with him appearing in 84 games, compiling a slash average of .235/.324/.368 with 7 home runs, 18 doubles and 42 RBI. He's signed with the Giants through 2030 after inking a six-year, $151 million contract extension in September 2024.

Despite the injury, Chapman was still outstanding defensively at third base. Advanced metrics credit him with 16 Defensive Runs Saved and 4 Outs Above Average.

In Chapman's absence, Christian Koss (.157 average, .380 OPS) has been filling in at third base. Casey Schmitt (21 homers, .784 OPS) likely would have taken over at the position, but he will also miss the rest of the season due to a torn meniscus sustained in July 27's 3-0 win over the Milwaukee Brewers that required surgery.

Another possibility might be Marcelo Mayer, the former Boston Red Sox prospect who the Giants picked up at the MLB trade deadline for left-handed reliever Erik Miller. Mayer, 23, is a natural shortstop but with Willy Adames manning that position, he may have to play elsewhere. Last season, Mayer played 39 games at third base, starting 28 of them.

Mayer is currently on the injured list with a bone stress reaction in his left forearm, but he's been cleared for baseball activities and could begin a minor-league rehab assignment next week.

title: Ole Miss football legend Archie Manning will get statue on campus
description: Ole Miss football legend Archie Manning will be honored with a statue on campus by the Manning Center, Ole Miss said.
fullText:
OXFORD — Ole Miss football legend Archie Manning will be getting a statue outside the Manning Center.

An Ole Miss spokesperson confirmed the news to the Clarion Ledger on Aug. 8, and said the school will have more information in the coming days.

Manning, 77, is one of the most revered figures in the history of the Ole Miss program. He was the star quarterback for Ole Miss from 1968-70 under coach Johnny Vaught. Manning also played baseball at Ole Miss.

Manning ended his Ole Miss career with 56 touchdowns, which was a school record, and 5,576 yards of total offense. He finished No. 3 in Heisman Trophy voting in 1970. He was a 1989 inductee into the College Football Hall of Fame and was drafted No. 2 overall by the New Orleans Saints in the 1971 NFL Draft.

Additionally, Manning is the father of NFL greats Peyton Manning and Eli Manning. Eli played for Ole Miss from 2000-03 and was third in Heisman Trophy voting in 2003. Archie Manning now runs the Manning Passing Academy with his sons.

Archie's grandson, Arch, is the quarterback for Texas and considered a frontrunner for the Heisman Trophy.

The Manning patriarch has already been honored on the Ole Miss campus in other ways. Speed limit signs on campus are 18 miles per hour, which is a nod to Archie's number for the Rebels. Ole Miss football practices in the Olivia and Archie Manning Athletics Performance Center.

Manning is the second Ole Miss football player to be honored with a statue. Chucky Mullins has a movable bust that is prominently featured on football game days in the Ole Miss tunnel. Mullins was paralyzed in a 1989 game and died in 1991 due to complications from the injury.

Vaught, Coolidge Ball and Tim Elko are other Ole Miss athletic statues on campus.

Vaught is Ole Miss' winningest football coach with 190 victories, and his statue was dedicated in 2008.

Ball was the first Black athlete at Ole Miss, playing basketball from 1971-74. His statue was unveiled in 2021.

Elko was a star player on the 2022 Ole Miss baseball team that won the College World Series. Elko's statue was unveiled in 2024.

Sam Hutchens covers Ole Miss for the Clarion Ledger. Email him at Shutchens@gannett.com or reach him on X at @Sam_Hutchens_

title: Why Florida dropped in ESPN's team recruiting rankings
description: A top-25 signing shifted ESPN's team recruiting rankings for the class of 2027. Here's where Florida now stands.
fullText:
Florida football dropped one spot to No. 8 in the 2027 ESPN team recruiting rankings on Thursday.

The movement is a result of Miami landing No. 25 overall recruit and top-ranked athlete A'Mir Sears. The Hurricanes jumped three spots from No. 8 to No. 5, pushing the Gators, Oklahoma Sooners (No. 6) and Ohio State Buckeyes (No. 7) down one spot each.

Almost every other team in the top 10 stayed put, with Texas A&M and Notre Dame at the top of the list. Oregon and Texas flipped spots to Nos. 3 and 4, respectively, while Auburn and Texas Tech held steady at Nos. 9 and 10.

There isn't a ton of room for further movement over the next few months. All but four of the recruits ranked on the ESPN 300 are committed. Florida only has an offer to one of them: four-star running back Caden Waye out of Ola High School in McDonough, Georgia.

Waye included Florida in his top 12 back in December, but interest in him has dropped for several national programs. His only official visit of the summer was to UCF, and his list now includes Texas State, UTEP, Louisiana Tech and Missouri State.

He may no longer be a take for the Gators with four-star running back Andrew Beard committed from the class. Still, adding him to the commitment list could improve Florida's standing on ESPN's ranking moving forward.

title: Kentucky fall sports season begins with weekend exhibition matches
description: The 2026 fall season of Kentucky Wildcats sports kicks off on Saturday with three exhibition matchups.
fullText:
The month of August is here, bringing with it the hottest part of the summer, the start of school for most, and the return of fall sports. College football is still a month away, but there are Kentucky Wildcats athletes who will be back in action on Saturday.

Things kick off with the return of the Kentucky women's volleyball squad. After falling in the national championship game last year, they're looking to rebound quickly, and have the talent to do so. Brooklyn DeLeye and Molly Tuozzo lead the way as they play in their first exhibition matchup of the year against Ohio University. That game will be at 5:00 P.M. ET with free admission. It won't be available on television, though.

Also at 5:00 P.M. ET will be the first exhibition match for the women's soccer team. They take on Lexington SC, and the admission is also free as part of Kentucky's Fan Day festivities. There will be a post-match autograph signing for interested fans.

Then, the day wraps up with the men's soccer team facing off against Northern Kentucky. That match is scheduled for 7:30 P.M. ET, depending on the finish of the women's match. As part of Fan Day, once again admission will be free, and an autograph session will follow.

It's an exciting time for college sports fans, who are encouraged to go support all three of these squads. We wish them good luck as they begin their 2026 seasons.

title: Survey results: Giants fans are feeling the optimism
description: Are NY Giants fans right to be optimistic about their team?
fullText:
The summer is the season for optimism around the NFL, the time when fans of every team allow themselves to indulge in hope for the coming season.

The New York Giants have had a bit more than a week of training camp and are about a week away from their first preseason game on August 15th. Rather than asking about anything specific before seeing the team on the field in a live situation, we wanted to take the temperature of the fanbase as things start to ramp up.

It isn't much of a surprise that the overwhelming majority of Giants fans are either optimistic, or outright excited, about their team. That flies in the face of the national perspective, where the Giants are an afterthought and even outright derided. Even Las Vegas views the Giants as extreme long-shots to make the playoffs this year, with the second-longest odds in the NFC, per FanDuel.

We'll see if the fans or the national perspective is right, but so far the news out of camp has been almost universally positive.

Camp under John Harbaugh has been faster and tougher than what we've seen in recent years from the Giants, with a much higher level of accountability.

The defense under Dennard Wilson has been consistently disruptive and at times dominant. The pass rush has been making the quarterbacks' lives difficult while the secondary hasn't been giving up much separation at all. And while they aren't hauling in all their interception opportunities, the defensive backs seem to be playing faster and more confidently than we saw the last two years.

The defense hasn't been allowing the offense to establish much rhythm or consistency, but we're still getting positive reports out of that side of the ball as well.

Both WR Malik Nabers and RB Cam Skattebo are healthier than many of us on the outside anticipated, and Odell Beckham Jr. has been rounding into form with increased reps. Rookie WR Malachi Fields has produced highlight reel catches with regularity, and the offensive line has looked good as well — despite the pass rush consistently getting into the backfield. It seems that's just a function of the Giants' hyper-athletic front seven, not poor play on the part of the blockers.

There are, of course, fans who aren't drinking the Big Blue kool-aid just yet — And that's fair. After all, the Giants looked amazing in camp and preseason last year, but still managed to snatch defeat from the jaws of victory on five separate occasions during the season.

We'll see how the good reports translate into the preseason, as well as how the Giants progress over their three preseason games. Last year there were consistent lapses in execution and assignment discipline that were never resolved and became the team's Achilles heel in the season. Even if the Giants don't win their preseason games, we'll see a solid baseline of execution and what issues that crop up be corrected.

title: How is former Auburn QB Ashton Daniels faring at FSU preseason camp?
description: The former Auburn starter is hoping to end his college career on a positive note at Florida State.
fullText:
Former Auburn quarterback Ashton Daniels produced solid numbers over the final portion of Auburn football's 2025 season. However, the Tigers' quarterback room was gutted with the hire of Alex Golesh, and Daniels was left needing to find a new home for his final season of eligibility.

He found that new home through the transfer portal in Tallahassee, Florida, and is poised to take over the starting quarterback role for Florida State in 2026. Florida State, like Auburn, is hungry to return to success this season, and Daniels will be tasked with leading the Seminoles to bowl eligibility for the first time since 2023.

How is Daniels faring in his new uniform? Florida State head coach Mike Norvell shared with the media this week that Daniels has shown signs of blemish, but is impressed with the former Tiger so far as the Seminoles prepare for the 2026 season.

"But he's been outstanding when it comes to knowing where to go with the ball, his ownership of the things we're asking him to do," Norvell said. "I would say it would challenge as good as what I've seen. Just the way that he's gone about that."

Since missing the 2023 College Football Playoff, Florida State has won just seven games over the last two seasons, and is working to return to the postseason picture. Daniels will get the chance to lead the Seminoles' offense and will rely on talented pieces, including wide receiver Duce Robinson, to achieve that goal.

Daniels initially lost the starting job to Jackson Arnold last season at Auburn, but made the most of his season by passing for 797 yards and three scores over the final four games of the 2026 season. He completed 49 passes for 612 yards over his final two starts against SEC rivals Vanderbilt and Alabama, throwing just one interception.

Daniels has proven during his time at Auburn and Stanford to be a quality passer, and worked to limit turnovers last season on the Plains. He will look to use his development as a senior for the Florida State Seminoles and end his collegiate career on a positive note.

title: Panthers fans react to Luke Kuechly being enshrined into the Pro Football Hall of Fame
description: Panthers fans were in celebration mode on Saturday, as franchise great Luke Kuechly was enshrined into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.
fullText:
When it comes to the Carolina Panthers, there are four greats who stand out above all others.

Cam Newton was the best quarterback in franchise history and their only Most Valuable Player award winner. Wide receiver Steve Smith captured the hearts of fans more than any other team legend. And the quiet giant Julius Peppers performed at a high level longer than anyone else.

All that being said, the guy who played his own position better than anyone else ever did was Luke Kuechly—arguably the best off-ball linebacker of his generation.

title: Mourinho to act as a ‘father figure’ to key Real Madrid superstar after fresh extension
description: Real Madrid put an end to Vinicius Jr.’s long-running transfer saga by extending his contract until 2032.The Brazilian has signed a lucrative contract that should seal his long-term future at Santia...
fullText:
Real Madrid put an end to Vinicius Jr.'s long-running transfer saga by extending his contract until 2032.

The Brazilian has signed a lucrative contract that should seal his long-term future at Santiago Bernabeu and it is evident the club want to keep him happy.

Vinicius has been an asset for Los Blancos over the years and Real Madrid are working hard to make sure the player feels at home, despite having made so many signings this summer.

According to El Larguero, Jose Mourinho is set to take Vinicius under his wing and act as a father figure to the Brazilian going forward.

Mourinho will back Vinicius at every turn. (Photo by Christian Bruna/Getty Images)

The report suggests Mourinho intends to be by Vinicius' side at all times, aware that the winger is a good but highly emotional character whose temperament has occasionally led him into trouble.

The Portuguese understands that, and believes his guidance can help the player channel his emotions more effectively.

Having previously held out for a package worth close to €30 million, the Brazilian ultimately accepted a €24 million base salary, boosted by significant bonuses, effectively choosing glory over money by turning down Arsenal's ambitious interest.

That father-figure relationship is no surprise given the part Mourinho reportedly played in getting the deal over the line.

Vinicius expected to play a key role at Real Madrid next season. (Photo by Angel Martinez/Getty Images)

The Portuguese was absolutely key to the renewal, directly intervening to ensure the player stayed.

Mourinho is said to have called Vinicius multiple times during the holidays to sell him on his project and open his mind to accepting Real Madrid's offer, with the pair also speaking regularly after training.

The two now share a strong relationship despite the fallout from last season's Champions League tie against Benfica, when Mourinho appeared to criticise the winger.

With the renewal secured, Vinicius will now look to justify the faith placed in him and rediscover his best form.

The immediate priority, however, will be improving his chemistry with Kylian Mbappe, which was surprisingly poor last season.

title: Flats left empty for nearly four years over claim
description: The council says the block of 34 flats is still not safe to occupy and an insurance claim is pending.
fullText:
A national housing charity says it is "sad" to see a block of flats that have been empty for nearly four years "going to waste".

Central Bedfordshire Council acquired Birch Court in Dunstable in October 2022, but it said the building was not safe to occupy.

The council was still waiting for an insurance claim to be processed to pay for repairs, years after surveys highlighted "critical defects" in the building that posed a potential fire safety risk.

Chris Bailey, director of policy and campaigns for Action on Empty Homes, said: "The situation with Birch Court is typical of far too many recently constructed or renovated buildings across the country."

"In Dunstable, as elsewhere, it's definitely a contributor to the rapidly rising number of empty homes," he added.

Steven Watkins, executive member for assets, business and housing at the council, said: "We recognise the frustration that it remains empty."

He added he wanted to see the building brought into use "as soon as possible".

The council owns the flats and the intention was for them to be available to people on its social housing waiting list, aged over 40.

The Council Taxbase 2025 data from the Empty Homes Network showed the East of England region had seen a rise in the number of empty homes over the past five years.

It reveals that 112,074 properties stood vacant last year - an increase of 15,896 since 2021.

Empty homes now account for about 4% of all dwellings in the region, closely matching the national average.

Meanwhile, government figures show the number of households in the country living in temporary accommodation is at a record high.

Action on Empty Homes questioned how much the council was spending on accommodation for homeless families while Birch Court remained empty.

The council has yet to respond to that question.

Watkins, an Independent councillor, said: "It would be premature to speculate on the future of the building at this stage, as the next steps will be determined once the insurance claim process is complete.

"We recognise the need for housing across Central Bedfordshire and remain committed to supporting local people in housing need, and we manage several thousand homes for local people."

title: Idaho bystander who distracted In-N-Out shooter speaks out
description: "While I am physically safe, my heart is heavy for our community and for everyone whose lives were changed forever," Braxton Steube wrote.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — Braxton Steube, the man credited with distracting the gunman on a nearby walking trail during a shooting at an In-N-Out in Idaho, says he's "still processing" coming into contact with the shooter.

"It was a terrifying and traumatic experience that I am still processing," Steube wrote in a Facebook post. "While I am physically safe, my heart is heavy for our community and for everyone whose lives were changed forever."

Steube says he encountered gunman Chad Williams on a walking trail and spoke with him. Video shows Williams shot at him but missed.

"I said, 'I have a family,'" he told KMVT-TV. "I said, 'You don't have to do this. I'll tell you whatever you want. I'll do anything.' He started to like tear up a bit, it seemed. And he said to me, 'Just get away from me, man.'"

Police are calling Steube a hero, as his actions likely helped others escape. They say he ran into Williams on the trail near the restaurant after fleeing a nearby Dicks Sporting Goods, where he worked.

"Your courage, your composure, your selflessness in that moment likely gave others the time they needed to escape harm," Twin Falls Police Chief Matthew Hicks said during a news conference. "This community is grateful for you, and we will never forget what you did that day."

"For this to happen in a town like Twin Falls is heartbreaking," Steube wrote in a post. "Our community has always been defined by care and compassion, and it is difficult to process that this occurred here."

Video released by the Twin Falls Police Department shows multiple bystanders intervening to help aid victims and attempt to subdue the shooter, who began shooting while at a drive-through window of the fast food chain before parking and shooting other victims, then moving through the parking lot area and toward a visitor center.

Other video footage shows bystanders helping to evacuate employees and patrons and rendering aid to those injured, with multiple former or off-duty law enforcement officers acting to try to help those at the scene and subdue the shooter.

NewsNation's Steph Whiteside contributed to this report.

title: Hunter Biden says his father's prostate cancer is causing him pain even as he continues to speak out
description: Former U.S. President Joe Biden ’s prostate cancer has spread to other parts of his body and is causing him pain, even as he continues to speak out on public issues, his son Hunter said in an intervie...
fullText:
LONDON (AP) — Former U.S. President Joe Biden 's prostate cancer has spread to other parts of his body and is causing him pain, even as he continues to speak out on public issues, his son Hunter said in an interview.

In a wide-ranging interview with the BBC broadcast late on Friday, Hunter Biden grew emotional as he discussed his father's condition, describing it as very sad to watch.

"The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further," he said. "It's very painful and it's very debilitating in many respects."

Joe Biden, 83, was the oldest man to serve as U.S. president and his age was a source of concern for much of his four years in office. He and his White House advisers have faced intense criticism for allegedly concealing the extent of his problems, especially after he was forced to abandon his bid for re-election after a disastrous debate with his eventual successor, Donald Trump.

The former president revealed his cancer diagnosis in May of last year, less than four months after he left the White House.

Hunter Biden said the diagnosis had been tough on the family.

"It's really sad to watch," Biden said. "The only thing that I'd say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it's not good."

But Biden said his father remains "out there," speaking publicly about the issues that are important to him.

"He's still doing his thing," he said. "He so believes in this country."

The former president will publish a memoir, "Promise Me, America," after the mid-term elections.

title: Former DNC Vice Chair David Hogg claims Democratic moderates 'don't have the right values'
description: Former DNC Vice Chair David Hogg told moderate Democrats they "don't have the right values" as progressive candidates score primary wins before 2026.
fullText:
Former Democratic National Committee Vice Chair David Hogg told moderate Democrats they "don't have the right values" Thursday during an appearance on "The Source," arguing the party establishment is repeatedly losing because its priorities are out of step with Americans as progressive candidates score primary victories ahead of the 2026 midterms.

Hogg made his sharpest criticism after host Kaitlan Collins asked what he would tell moderates concerned that progressive nominees could struggle against Republicans in general elections.

"The reason why the establishment of our party is being defeated over and over and over again is because they don't have the right values that are aligned with not the Democratic base, but the American people," Hogg said. "Where people are sick and tired of listening to Democrats and tell them all the reasons why they can't solve their problems."

2026 Midterms State Of Play: Key Races Unfold As Stevens, El-sayed Battle In Michigan

Hogg told moderates they needed to change their approach rather than ask successful progressive candidates to move toward the center.

"I would say to the moderates in our party, 'You need to figure out how to actually offer something new to voters that isn't just the same message that you gave them in 2024,'" Hogg said.

Steven Bonnell II, the liberal streamer known as "Destiny," pushed back on Hogg's assessment in a statement to Fox News Digital, saying he does not believe the former DNC official represents rank-and-file Democrats.

"I would say that this is outside of the Democratic Party's mainstream views," Destiny said. "Polls seem to evidence this, with a plurality (or majority, in some cases) of Democratic voters feeling as though the party has moved too far to the left."

Rahm Emanuel Warns Dsa Agenda Doesn't Play Well Outside 'Upper West Side Of Manhattan'

Destiny, who has repeatedly criticized the party's far-left socialist wing, said Hogg's comments were an example of a dynamic that allows progressives to attack moderates without facing similar scrutiny from within the party.

"People in the Democratic Party's extreme fringe have created a 'ratchet effect,' where you cannot criticize anyone to the left-of-moderate view point," Destiny said. "Those same people can infinitely attack the moderate wing, leading outsiders (and even people from within) to view the Democratic Party as far more extreme than it actually is."

He warned that a Democratic Party that decides its moderates do not share its values could face consequences at the ballot box.

"I think it would mean the Democratic Party would probably have a hugely difficult time succeeding in the upcoming general in 2028 and possibly even stumble in 2026," Destiny said. "Which is especially ridiculous given how low Trump's popularity is at the moment."

Sen Mark Kelly Warns Far-left Policies That 'Don't Make Sense' Could Cost Democrats Seats

Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville has taken the opposite side of the party's ideological battle, telling Fox News Digital Thursday that Democratic primary voters would ultimately reject the socialist wing.

"I think it's more likely than not that the Democrats embrace sanity," Carville said.

Carville said a takeover by the socialist wing could ultimately fracture the party, reiterating comments he has made amid the growing influence of figures including self-described socialist streamer Hasan Piker.

"That probably would result in some kind of schism in the party," Carville said. "I'm going to let Democratic voters determine the direction that party goes in, and if it goes in the direction — which I'm pretty confident it won't — but if it goes in that direction, then I'm going to be 82. OK, fine, go ahead, but not with me."

Carville has also said he would leave the party if Piker became a significant force within it, while Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., responded that Carville could "start his own party."

Fox News Digital reached out to the DNC for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

Fox News Digital's Alexander Hall contributed to this article.

title: Norwegian soldiers say they're training Ukrainian soldiers with a 'Viking mentality' built for harsh conditions
description: Norwegian troops are bringing battlefield skills and a Viking-inspired warrior mentality to training Ukrainian soldiers on NATO soil.
fullText:
Norwegian troops are bringing a Viking-inspired warrior culture into their training of Ukrainian soldiers.

The Telemark Battalion uses harsh training to build cohesion, discipline, and resilience.

Ukraine is also shaping the program and sharing its battlefield expertise with NATO.

Norwegian soldiers are bringing their own "Viking mentality" and warrior culture to the training of Ukrainian troops for war with Russia.

Norway is leading Operation Legio, a new international effort to support, train, and equip Ukrainian soldiers for the fight. Battlefield training combines Ukrainian combat experience with NATO warfighting practices.

The training, supported by 11 nations, is primarily conducted by personnel from the Telemark Battalion, an elite mechanized infantry battalion of the Norwegian Army that has made aspects of Viking culture central to its identity.

Maj. John, the S3 Operations Officer in charge of synchronizing the overall training operation, told Business Insider that Norway's Telemark Battalion puts great emphasis on building skills, but also developing a "warrior mentality" that allows them to fight and "thrive in harsh conditions."

"We draw that warrior mentality from our Viking heritage," he said, "and the Viking culture is very important for us." He asked to only be identified by his first name for security reasons.

The elite battalion, which has deployed on combat missions in places like the Balkans, Afghanistan, and Iraq, is represented by the emblem of a Viking ship, and the unit's Viking-inspired battle cry is: "To Valhalla!" In Norse mythology, Valhalla is the great hall in Asgard for brave warriors slain in battle.

John said the battalion's mindset is "not like over-aggressive, over-eager, doing stupid stuff. We take the best parts of that Viking mentality and then apply it to the ethical and moral standards that are required of our soldiers."

John said the training emphasizes both battlefield skills and the "warrior mentality" and discipline needed to "thrive in harsh conditions."

"It's a mix between skills and mentality," he said.

The Ukrainians arriving for training are not necessarily novices when it comes to enduring harsh conditions. Many of them come from a military shaped by years of high-intensity warfare, and Norwegian leaders repeatedly described the training as an exchange in which Ukraine's combat experience shapes what its NATO partners teach.

The way the Norwegians reinforce their approach, John said, is "through exposing them to harsh training." The training, conducted at a camp in southeastern Poland, is designed to be tough, with daytime and nighttime operations and scenarios intended to replicate battlefield conditions as closely as possible.

Brigadier Atle Molde, commander of Task Force Legio, doesn't currently serve in the Telemark battalion, but he said of this unit that "they have their culture, and of course, a warrior mentality is a good thing as long as it drives unit cohesion and fighting for something common."

Even the training camp, a purpose-built training site in Poland, roughly two hours from Ukraine's border, reflects that Viking identity.

Camp Jomsborg was established in 2025, and it began its fifth 51-day rotation of Ukrainian soldiers in late May. Norway acts as the framework nation, providing the main structure and leadership for the other participating countries.

"It's all about the Ukrainian soldier and increasing his lethality and survivability within this program before he leaves for front-line war," said John. The main goal, he said, is supporting Ukraine so it can keep defending itself and win the war on its own or negotiate a peace agreement on its own terms.

The name Camp Jomsborg comes from the legendary Viking fortress Jomsborg. Molde said that what characterized the Jomsvikings, a legendary warrior brotherhood based along the Baltic Sea, "was that they were very disciplined and professional warriors. So that's where the name comes from."

That history is visible throughout the camp, which Business Insider visited. Viking-inspired signs and a large Viking ship decorate the huge, purpose-built site where soldiers train, eat, and sleep. There are other references to Norwegian culture, too, with its streets named after figures like Thor, the Norse god of thunder.

Molde said that "unit cohesion is important," and that the Telemark Battalion was seeking to take what it sees as positive in its own culture and "try to give that over to the Ukrainians as well. So long as it has a positive effect, it's a good thing."

Plus, he said, "for one reason or another, the whole Viking mythology, the Ukrainians like that."

Ukraine's military and civilian population have shown extraordinary resilience under years of sustained Russian attacks against not just military targets, but civilian ones as well. Western leaders have repeatedly said that Moscow is seeking to break Ukraine's spirit and willingness to resist and force it into submission. Instead, Ukraine has continued fighting and adapting, developing battlefield innovations and tactics that its Western partners increasingly want to study and learn from.

Ukraine's military and population are enduring conditions that no Western country has experienced in decades, including heavy attrition, constant attacks, and enormous losses.

Ukraine's battlefield experience and expertise are central to the Legio training operation. "We have defined this as a Ukrainian training center," John said.

Ukraine outlines what it needs and wants to learn, and its partners structure the training around those requirements, with Ukrainian instructors also helping to lead. The program was built around Ukrainian requests and expertise and is regularly updated based on Ukrainian feedback.

Defining it that way means Ukraine can "hold us accountable for quality and delivering that realistic training," John said. That cooperation, he said, "is what has made this an effective training mission."

Many of the Ukrainians at Camp Jomsborg have real-world lessons from brutal warfare that their instructors lack, while Western trainers have decades of institutional experience and NATO practices to offer in return. Molde said it's a case of everyone working together to combine those strengths and learn from one another.

Jørgen, a Norwegian instructor at the camp, told Business Insider that training the Ukrainians isn't difficult. "I think it's quite incredible how eager to learn they are in general," he said. "It kind of confirms how good the guys are."

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Autism providers cheer Trump crackdown after millions allegedly stolen from children through Medicaid fraud
description: Autism care providers back the Trump administration's Medicaid fraud crackdown but warn policymakers not to create barriers for families of autistic children.
fullText:
FIRST ON FOX: American autism care providers are backing the Trump administration's crackdown on Medicaid fraud, arguing that the alleged theft of millions of federal funds has hurt both taxpayers and children with autism who rely on those services.

A coalition of autism clinicians, behavioral therapists and families of children with autism are speaking out in favor of the administration's efforts to hold people accountable for the suspected exploitation of the Medicaid system.

The group — the Autism Families Alliance — describes itself as a national advocacy organization dedicated to supporting Applied Behavior Analysis providers and the families who rely on their services. It aims to ensure that every child and family has access to high-quality care without unnecessary barriers, reduced access or funding cuts.

"We do this work because we believe every child deserves the chance to communicate, gain independence, and live the fullest life possible," Taylor Sanders, a family advocate at the Autism Families Alliance, told Fox News Digital. "I've worked with children who found their voice after being nonverbal. I've watched families go from fear and uncertainty to hope because their child was finally making progress. Those are the moments that keep us going. That's why we're here."

Watch: Dr. Oz Says Newsom, Other Blue States Have Turned Medicaid Fraud Into A 'Feature'

"President Trump and the administration are right: fraud is unacceptable and those responsible should be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law," Sanders added.

The group argues that every dollar allegedly stolen by fraudsters should have been used to help a child with autism learn to communicate, gain independence and receive the care they need.

The members strongly support eliminating fraud and prosecuting suspected criminals, but they also fear that broad federal and state efforts to root out fraud could unintentionally make it more difficult for legitimate providers to care for children with autism.

Some states, including Georgia, North Carolina and Indiana, have taken steps to enhance oversight of autism services.

But the coalition is calling on policymakers to ensure fraudsters are removed from the system without creating what they describe as unnecessary barriers for families of vulnerable children seeking care.

"There's real concern among the families I work with that their children's care could be interrupted because of the government's response to these criminals," Sanders said. "Access to these programs aren't a political talking point to these families, it's their lifeline. Losing this lifeline is a real fear that parents worry about every day. As some states move to crack down on fraud, we have to make sure we're targeting fraudsters, not putting new barriers in front of families trying to get their children the care they need."

The coalition's stance on the administration's fraud crackdown echoes comments made recently by Dr. Mehmet Oz, who serves as administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services.

Read: Dr. Oz Puts All 50 Governors On Notice Over Billions Lost To Medicaid Fraud

"The good news is, our biggest allies are the folks who are doing it right," Oz said at a press briefing earlier this year as part of an announcement of a sweeping national anti-fraud initiative targeting multi-billion dollar Medicaid and Medicare leakage across various states.

"They are the people who are doing hospice right, home healthcare right, who are doing all the things that we need for autism in this country. Those people come to us actually frustrated, angry that we're allowing, tolerating fraudsters who not only hurt people they care about but are stealing their business inappropriately," he said at the time.

Rocio Berni, the mother of an autistic child, Manny, in Charlotte, North Carolina, spoke about how her child has benefited from ABA providers.

"Working alongside ABA therapy providers has been immensely beneficial for my son," she told Fox News Digital. "Manny struggled with tantrums, and while he loved being around other children, he was frustrated by his inability to communicate with them."

"Today, through the work of dedicated therapists, we have learned to better regulate his behavior," she continued. "My son is now able to approach other children, and we hope he will be able to carry on basic, fulfilling conversations. I simply can't imagine what his life would be like without this care. I pray that policymakers will ensure that Manny and children like him maintain access to this essential care."

Kelsey Bennett, also a family advocate at the Autism Families Alliance, said fraud has "no place" in healthcare, emphasizing that ABA is "no exception."

"As a practicing clinician, it is disheartening to see the actions of a small number of bad actors cast a shadow over the thousands of ethical clinicians who have dedicated their careers to improving the lives of children with autism and their families," she told Fox News Digital.

Bennett said she backs moves to hold fraudsters accountable, but warned that those targets must be carefully pursued.

"We fully support efforts to identify and hold accountable those who engage in fraudulent billing, improper claims, or substandard care," Bennett said. "Fraud harms taxpayers, undermines trust in the healthcare system, damages the reputation of legitimate providers, and, most importantly, puts vulnerable children at risk."

"At the same time, efforts to combat fraud must be carefully targeted," she continued. "Policies designed to stop abuse should focus on those responsible without creating unnecessary barriers for families seeking medically necessary services. For children with autism, consistency and continuity of care are critical to long-term progress, and significantly limiting telehealth for supervision and assessments can further restrict access for families in rural and underserved areas. Families should not have to worry that broad policy changes or administrative burdens will interrupt the treatment their children rely on."

"The overwhelming majority of ABA providers are committed to providing high-quality, evidence-based care with integrity," she added. "Effective policy should protect public resources by eliminating fraud while preserving timely access to medically necessary treatment for the children and families these programs were created to serve. Children with autism should never bear the consequences of the unethical actions of a small minority of providers."

title: 34,000 texts found on Fauci’s COVID-era phone, Sen. Johnson says
description: He added there were also more than 500 voicemail messages, dating from about 2014 up to December 2022.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — A copy of Dr. Anthony Fauci's pandemic-era cellphone was handed over to a key investigative panel to uncover more records about Fauci's handling of the pandemic and the origin of the COVID-19 virus.

Wisconsin Republican Sen. Ron Johnson told NewsNation on Friday there are more than 34,000 text messages on Fauci's COVID-era cellphone; the Senate investigations subcommittee chaired by Johnson now has a copy of them.

He added there were also more than 500 voicemail messages, dating from about 2014 up to a few days before Fauci left the National Institutes of Health in December 2022.

"I can't and my staff can't guarantee that everything was preserved. What is odd is most of those text messages are associated with a phone number. He only had three contacts, which is pretty odd," Johnson said.

Investigators are searching for evidence of deleted files and private communications that contradict what Fauci said publicly. A copy of the phone was transferred from the Department of Health and Human Services to the Senate subcommittee.

"This is not going to be a document dump," Johnson said. "I also need to preserve documents for our investigation. We are interviewing other people that he may be texting. And if you're going to get truthful answers out of people, you can't necessarily show them all your all your investigatory material, as well.

"So, again, I'm not going to hold this close to the vest when there are things that the public needs to see. I'm hoping to work very closely with Senator Rand Paul and his staff and release these things jointly.

The Senate Panel for Security and Governmental Affairs voted 8-5 to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress on Thursday after he repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment during a hearing.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., referred the matter to the Justice Department, arguing Fauci's prior pardon by former President Joe Biden raises questions about whether Fauci could properly invoke that protection.

"I certainly think he should be on contempt of Congress charges, but mainly because not only did he show contempt for Congress, for our committee, for our investigation, he's shown utter contempt for the American public," Johnson told "Katie Pavlich Tonight."

" I think Anthony Fauci does face legal jeopardy in a number of different areas. But from my standpoint, the most important part of accountability is exposure, exposing who Anthony Fauci is, what he did. Let's face it, he was the primary director of our miserably failed response to COVID," Johnson said.

title: 'Deliberate and serious' waste dump found in field
description: An appeal for witnesses has been made by local officials after the pile was discovered.
fullText:
A huge pile of rubbish found dumped in a field in Leicestershire has been described by officials as a "serious and deliberate act of waste crime".

Hinckley and Bosworth Borough Council said a large amount of waste had been dumped on its land off the A47 Leicester Road between Hinckley and Earl Shilton.

A spokesperson for the authority said the waste appeared to be the "contents of household skips" and evidence from the site suggested heavy goods equipment had been used to hide the waste with soil.

Two vehicles found on the site have been removed under local authority powers for vehicles suspected of being used in waste crime, the council added.

Council leader Stuart Bray said: "This is a serious and deliberate act of waste crime.

"Those responsible have not only dumped a large amount of waste, they have taken steps to hide what they were doing.

"That makes it even more important that anyone who saw something unusual comes forward.

"We know residents will rightly be angry to see the countryside treated in this way.

"Our officers are working closely with the police and Environment Agency, and action has already been taken, including removing two vehicles from the site."

The council said the waste dump had been reported to the Environment Agency.

title: Bill Ackman’s $35 billion hedge fund has under 50 employees and all of them — from janitors to receptionists — own millions in company stock
description: Billionaire investor Bill Ackman says employee loyalty pays dividends—and he's willing to invest millions in stock awards and allowing summer remote work to earn it.
fullText:
Staying at one company for decades was once a badge of honor. But as layoffs have become more common and workers have turned to job hopping for higher pay and career growth, employee loyalty has become harder to find. Billionaire investor Bill Ackman, however, still believes earning employee loyalty is worth every penny.

That's why his hedge fund Pershing Square, which manages roughly $35 billion in assets, offers its four dozen employees generous workplace benefits, including broad ownership and an even rare degree of flexibility for Wall Street.

"There's not a person at Pershing Square that doesn't own multiple millions of dollars of stock in the company—whether you're cleaning the space or at the front desk or another role in the company," Ackman told Fortune's Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell on a recent episode of Fortune's Titans and Disruptors of Industry podcast. "We believe in taking care of our people."

Ackman's approach to retention goes beyond financial incentives. While Perishing employees are required to work from the office five days a week—that policy only applies for 10 months of the year. During July and August, employees can spread out as they like, with the company's investment team moving to the Hamptons together, either in homes they rent or own, to work.

"We look after people, and so that when you operate that way, people don't think about going anyplace else," Ackman said.

Pershing also invests heavily in employees' health and well-being, Ackman said, offering everything from healthy meals in its cafe to gym access and comprehensive healthcare benefits. With a staff of just 48 people, Pershing has not had one "undesired departure" from the firm.

"I think everyone here feels accurately that they're a big contributor to our success, and the result is we can accomplish an enormous amount," Ackman added.

Ackman grew up in New York before graduating from Harvard with his bachelor's in 1988 and later, his MBA in 1992. That year, he founded Gotham Partners with fellow Harvard graduate David P. Berkowitz, but the investment firm later failed in part after its bets on private companies backfired.

In 2004, he launched Pershing Square Capital Management, the activist hedge fund that has grown into one of Wall Street's best-known investment firms. Since its founding, Pershing has built major stakes in companies including Chipotle, Universal Music Group, and J.C. Penney. The firm went public on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange in 2014.

title: Berkshire Hathaway's new CEO Greg Abel spends a chunk of the company's massive cashpile
description: Berkshire Hathaway's new CEO Greg Abel spent a significant chunk of the company's massive pile of cash as it invested $10 billion in Google's parent company and repurchased about $4.5 billion of its shares.  The conglomerate that legendary investor Warren Buffett built reported its second-quarter earnings Saturday morning and disclosed that its cash holdings had shrunk to $365.5 billion from nearly $400 billion at the end of March.  Berkshire's report suggested that it had added more than $21 billion worth of commercial, industrial and other stocks to its portfolio, but the earnings report doesn't name the stocks it bought.
fullText:
OMAHA, Neb. (AP) — Berkshire Hathaway's new CEO Greg Abel spent a significant chunk of the company's massive pile of cash as it invested $10 billion in Google's parent company and repurchased about $4.5 billion of its shares.

The conglomerate that legendary investor Warren Buffett built reported its second-quarter earnings Saturday morning and disclosed that its cash holdings had shrunk to $365.5 billion from nearly $400 billion at the end of March.

Berkshire's report suggested that it had added more than $21 billion worth of commercial, industrial and other stocks to its portfolio, but the earnings report doesn't name the stocks it bought. That won't be revealed until a separate filing later this month.

Abel took over as CEO in January when Buffett retired after six decades leading the company. But Buffett remains chairman.

CFRA Research analyst Cathy Seifert said investors should be encouraged by the amount of shares Berkshire's repurchased although Geico's performance was a concern because its underwriting profits fell 45% and lagged far behind other big auto insurers.

"I think there are two key takeaways that should encourage investors: The fact that they bought back shares after not having done things of this magnitude for several years now. And the other positive thing is the ability to produce the 10% operating revenue growth in the quarter," Seifert said.

Abel announced in March that Berkshire had resumed buying back its own shares for the first time in more than two years, but investors were underwhelmed when the company only repurchased about $234 million worth of Berkshire stock in the first quarter.

The purchases in the second quarter that were disclosed Saturday demonstrate that Berkshire is serious about buybacks, but it is on the low end of the range that investors were expecting. Buffett watchers had been predicting repurchases somewhere between $5 billion and $11 billion based on a filing Buffett made when he announced his annual charitably donations in July.

The company's standard is that it only repurchases shares when Abel and Buffett believes they are selling for less than they are worth. They do not plan to spend a specific amount like many companies do. Most of Berkshire's repurchases were made in June. They may not be buying much now as the stock just hit a new 52-week high on Thursday.

Berkshire previously repurchased $78 billion worth of its own stock between 2018 and 2024.

In addition to the Google stock Berkshire bought this spring, the Omaha, Nebraska-based company also completed a $6.8 billion acquisition of homebuilder Taylor Morrison but that didn't close until July so it's not reflected in these quarterly figures.

title: Meet the 33-year-old CEO betting on boomers chasing their grandkids—and millennials selling their first house
description: "Consumers are starved for better tools to help make one of the biggest financial decisions of their life," says Kelley Blue Book Homes CEO John Liss.
fullText:
Kelley Blue Book built its reputation on a promise: a number you could trust because the people giving it to you had no stake in whether you bought or sold. John Liss is betting that promise will travel from cars to houses.

Liss is the 33-year-old CEO of both True Footage, the appraisal-technology company he founded at 26, and its new joint venture with Cox Enterprises: Kelley Blue Book Homes, which launched nationally across 11 states on Aug. 3.

He was a real estate agent in high school. Fifteen years — and multiple Harvard degrees — later, he is persuading one of America's most trusted consumer brands to put its name on a housing market where, by his own account, almost nobody trusts the numbers anymore.

"The available options are not accurate. They're not interpretable. They're not credible," Liss told Fortune. "Consumers are starved for better tools to help make one of the biggest financial decisions of their life."

The platform is built for two very different Americans converging on the housing market at the same moment. The first are what housing researchers call "baby chasers" — retirees relocating to be near grandchildren. Baby boomers are now the single largest cohort of both buyers and sellers nationally, accounting for roughly 42% of purchases and 55% of sales according to National Association of Realtors data.

"You have this sort of 'baby chaser' cohort," Liss said. "They've been in a house for a long time and they need to figure out the best strategy for how to sell their house and maximize their equity so they can move to wherever they've got to go, to be near their kids."

The second group doesn't have an industry-standard name yet. Liss offered "first-time sellers" — underbought millennials "bursting at the seams," squeezed by high mortgage rates into starter homes they can no longer fit. "Maybe they had that third kid and they need to get out of their house," he said. "They've never sold a house before. It's a confusing process. There's a lot of landmines."

The NAR puts the median first-time buyer age at a record 40, and an April 2026 Fortune analysis found older millennials increasingly behaving like boomers in the market — flush with cash, highly competitive buyers — even as boomers themselves continued to dominate transactions on the strength of decades of accumulated home equity.

True Footage says its TrueTracts appraisal engine can land a valuation within 3% of a home's eventual sale price — a claim drawn from KBB's own early test markets and not yet independently verified. In those markets, more than 17% of homeowners who received a valuation ended up listing on the MLS within 90 days, though the company has not disclosed a comparison baseline.

title: Schumer said ‘Democrats support voter ID’ — then every Senate Democrat voted against GOP bill
description: Chuck Schumer and Senate Democrats blocked Jon Husted's voter ID bill despite Schumer's past claims that Democrats support voter identification.
fullText:
Senate Democrats blocked a key component of the SAVE America Act that, in the past, they have supported.

During the wee hours of Saturday morning, Senate Republicans tried and failed to get Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., and his colleagues to back a stripped back voter ID bill amid a spree of last-minute legislative business.

But Senate Democrats, including Schumer, have for years espoused support for identification to vote. Several states with Democratic senators have voter ID laws, too.

Schumer, Democrats Say They Support Voter Id, Then Block Gop Amendment To Require It

"Democrats support voter ID," Schumer said in March. "In fact, we included it, and it is included, in our Freedom to Vote legislation several years ago."

Schumer and his entire caucus voted against the bill from Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, nonetheless. Requiring identification is already the practice in 36 states. Of those, 23 require photo ID, while 13 accept another form of identification, such as a bank statement. Nine of those states have Democratic senators.

It was the last stand of the night for the Senate, which is gearing up to leave Washington, D.C., for several weeks of valuable campaign time in vulnerable incumbents' home states.

Senate Republicans Push Election Day Deadline For California's Marathon Ballot Counts

And it comes as Republicans have so far tried and failed to find a path forward for the SAVE America Act, which Democrats, along with a handful from the GOP, have blocked numerous times in a variety of configurations.

Husted's bill would have prohibited state and local election officials from providing a ballot to vote in federal elections unless a person provided a valid form of identification.

Husted's bill teed up a plethora of options, including an unexpired driver's license with a photo, an unexpired state-issued ID card with a photo, a valid passport, a valid military or veteran ID with a photo or an unexpired tribal ID with a photo.

It's also not the first time Democrats have blocked it. In March, Republicans tested their support of voter ID for the first time in a vote to attach Husted's bill to the SAVE America Act. It failed on party lines then, too.

Trump Keeps Calling Thune Despite Public Fight Over Save America Act

After it became clear that President Donald Trump's top legislative priority was not going to be passed nor even considered before lawmakers exit Washington, D.C., Republicans opted to take one last crack at Democrats' resolve.

"We've got many Democrats, who have said, 'I'm just fine with voter ID,'" Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, said. "Voter ID is a major component of SAVE America, and they've said that over and over again when we had it on the floor in late February and early March."

"It was the argument that I heard from many of these people, as it was on the floor for hours and hours at a time, saying, 'I'm okay with voter ID, don't like this,'" he continued. "So we're gonna find out where they are."

Lee has been the loudest supporter of the SAVE America Act in the Senate, pushing and prodding his colleagues on X to get on board with passing the package.

Republicans had a chance earlier in the night to begin the work of crafting a version of the SAVE America Act with a budget blueprint that, if successful, would have teed up the partyline budget reconciliation process, but were called to stand down by Trump.

Now, they don't return until early September, just weeks out from a midterm election that could reshape the balance of power in the Senate.

title: Democrats plan Trump investigations over impeachment if they win House, sources say
description: U.S.
fullText:
WASHINGTON, Aug 8 (Reuters) - U.S. House Democrats preparing for a possible return to power are developing a broad investigative strategy targeting companies and financial firms surrounding President Donald Trump, instead of trying to impeach him immediately, according to four people familiar with the discussions.

Senior Democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives and committee aides have discussed using hearings, subpoenas and document ‌requests to obtain records from entities tied to Trump's political and business orbit, the sources said. It is a bet that investigating private companies and outside financial players will prove more fruitful than directly ‌confronting a White House they expect to resist oversight, they said.

The approach reflects both Democratic caution and a lesson many in the party say they learned during Trump's first term: that impeachment proceedings can consume Congress while allowing Trump to cast himself as the victim of a ​partisan campaign.

Instead, Democrats involved in the planning envision using House investigative powers after November's midterm elections to scrutinize the administration's decision-making and examine whether Trump used his power to benefit himself, allies or donors.

"We're not going into this to impeach," said a senior Democratic aide, describing the thinking among party leaders and committee staff. "No one wants a failed vote on day one. The focus is on building a body of evidence through investigations that can hold Trump accountable."

Republicans hold a narrow House majority, and polls favor Democrats regaining the majority in November. Winning control would give Democrats the power to issue subpoenas, compel testimony and documents, hold public hearings and pursue contempt proceedings.

Democrats expect the White House to fight or ignore requests ‌aimed at the executive branch, making companies, contractors and financial firms working with ⁠the administration an important route for obtaining information, the sources said.

The White House said in a statement that Trump has worked to thwart the "radical left's agenda" and remains committed to preserving Republican majorities in Congress. A White House official said the administration is "prepared to respond to oversight requests, no matter who is in the House or Senate."

Three sources said Apple, ⁠Alphabet, Palantir, Blackstone, BlackRock and companies owned by Elon Musk, such as Tesla, have surfaced in discussions because of their contracts, regulatory exposure or administration dealings. The sources said no final target list has been established and no formal investigations have begun.

The sources provided no further details about the investigations. Reuters could not determine if they face any accusations of wrongdoing.

Alphabet, Palantir, Blackstone and BlackRock declined comment. Apple and Tesla did not respond to a request for comment.

Democrats are expected to examine Department of Homeland ​Security ​contracts, financing for Trump's planned White House ballroom, corporate donors and alleged pay-to-play arrangements, two sources said. They also plan a probe ​of Trump-linked financial vehicles including 1789 Capital - a venture capital firm where his son ‌Donald Trump Jr. is a partner - and foreign sovereign wealth funds whose investments in Trump family-linked entities could raise questions about administration influence, the sources said.

1789 Capital did not respond to a request for comment.

Because foreign funds may be harder for congressional committees to reach, Democrats are discussing seeking records from U.S.-based firms and funds tied to Trump's family and other intermediaries, the two sources said.

Democrats have already begun laying the groundwork for investigations, two of the sources said.

Party leaders are sending letters to companies, contractors and other organizations connected to potential investigations, they said. The requests seek records and pave the way for subpoenas if Democrats win the House, the two sources said.

Representatives Robert Garcia from California and Jamie Raskin from Maryland, the top Democrats on the House Oversight and Judiciary Committees, respectively, said existing investigations would expand if Democrats win the House.

"From sketchy Pentagon contracts lining the pockets of the president's sons, ‌Trump's crypto billions, and the shady backroom deals for Trump donors, we will ensure we combat corruption when Democrats take back the ​House in November," Garcia said in a statement.

The letters include requests for information from media company Paramount Skydance over its dealings with ​the Trump administration and the proposed Warner Bros. Discovery deal as well as video platform YouTube and parent ​company Alphabet over the company's $24.5 million settlement with Trump in September. Letters have also been sent to private prison operator GEO Group and security firm Salus Worldwide Solutions for their ‌contracts with the DHS as well as commodity traders Vitol and Trafigura over the ​administration's sale of Venezuelan oil, the two sources said.

Alphabet and ​Trafigura declined comment. The others did not respond to requests for comment.

The companies can ignore the requests while Democrats are in the minority. But the letters put potential targets on notice and signal records Democrats could subpoena, the two sources said.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said in June on NBC's "Meet the Press" that Democrats haven't ruled out impeaching Trump if they win back the House but that the ​party's focus would be on pocketbook issues.

Democrats involved in the planning say impeachment remains ‌an option if investigations uncover evidence of an impeachable offense, but not as a first move.

The calculation reflects the party's experience during Trump's first term, when he became the first U.S. president to be ​impeached twice by the House before being acquitted by the Senate each time.

"If investigations uncover evidence that we believe meets the threshold, we will not hesitate to move forward," said the senior ​Democratic aide.

title: US expects deal soon on Strait of Hormuz; Sunni powers unite in defense pact
description: WASHINGTON/RIYADH, Aug 7 (Reuters) - A U. official on Friday reported progress between Iran and Oman that could soon reopen the Strait of Hormuz, potentially restoring oil exports that have been disru...
fullText:
WASHINGTON/RIYADH, Aug 7 (Reuters) - A U.S. official on Friday reported progress between Iran and Oman that could soon reopen the Strait of Hormuz, potentially restoring oil exports that have been disrupted by the five-month-old U.S. war with Iran.

The U.S. official, who declined to be identified, said Washington anticipated an agreement ‌soon between the two countries, which sit on either side of the strait, so that normal oil traffic could resume.

A deal between Iran and Oman over control of ‌the strategic waterway is seen as crucial to a wider peace agreement.

"There is progress between Oman and Iran on the strait, and we expect a deal soon," a U.S. official told Reuters on Friday. "Once the deal is announced to restore ​commercial shipping without impediments, the United States will lift the blockade of Iranian ports."

"As always, U.S. actions will continue to be performance-based and tied to Iran's implementation of its commitments," the official said.

Before the U.S. and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28, about one out of every five barrels of oil consumed worldwide transited the strait, but Iran has used the hostilities to justify charging a toll on oil tankers and firing on ships that attempt to cross the strait without permission.

That disruption in oil shipments has caused energy prices to surge and fueled inflation.

In recent weeks, the Trump administration ‌has repeatedly signaled that a deal to open the strait could ⁠be close, only to have Iran deny that talks are under way. It was unclear whether the latest flurry of negotiations would yield a more lasting arrangement.

Iranian strikes on Strait of Hormuz shipping have been coupled with increased attacks by its Yemen-based allies, the Houthis, who have targeted ships at ⁠another oil chokepoint on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula between the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

Abu Dhabi National Oil Company, one of the world's largest energy producers, said on Friday that 15 of its vessels had been struck in what it called unprovoked attacks while transiting the Strait of Hormuz since the start of the conflict. The attacks have killed one crew member and wounded 20 others, it said.

Alarmed at a regional conflagration that has brought Iranian missile fire onto Gulf oil exporters, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and ​Turkey signed a joint defense agreement in Mecca on Friday.

The pact among ‌three U.S. allies with majority Sunni Muslim populations is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as an attack on all, the countries said in a statement.

Turkey said the agreement was not aimed at any specific country and was purely defensive. But it comes at a time of heightened tensions with Shi'ite-majority Iran.

Meanwhile, the U.S. has been trying to broker an end to fighting on another front of the war between Israel and Iranian-backed Shi'ite group Hezbollah in southern Lebanon.

A Lebanese official said on Friday that Lebanon and Israel agreed on a shortlist of countries that could send troops to verify the disarmament of Hezbollah under a U.S.-brokered agreement. The United States would pick countries from the ‌list.

IRAN PRESIDENT DEFENDS DIPLOMACY

Washington and Tehran have not engaged in direct high-level talks since U.S. Vice President JD ​Vance met Iranian officials in Switzerland in June, shortly after the two sides reached a ceasefire agreement. That short-lived ​June 17 memorandum of understanding established terms for resuming Strait of Hormuz oil shipping and ​led to a ceasefire.

Amid internal opposition to the deal in the U.S. and Iran, hostilities resumed on July 7, only to be put on hold ‌again. The U.S. military's Central Command has not reported any strikes on ​Iran since July 29.

Analysts have said signs of fissures ​between Iran's civilian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, and the other power centers in Iran, notably Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, may be complicating peace efforts.

In an interview with state television broadcast on Friday, Pezeshkian defended his government's policies against hardliners who have opposed negotiations with the United States. He said that most senior military ​commanders supported talks towards a deal to stop the fighting.

"America's biggest ‌enemy is China, why don't they fight? China is doing its own thing and is getting stronger day by day. When we can get our rights through dialogue, ​why not do it?" he said.

title: How Scott Bessent used financial engineering to finance the $2 trillion deficit while leaving it untouched—and created a $1.45 trillion shortfall
description: The alarm is coming from inside the house. The Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee says the borrowing math no longer adds up.
fullText:
While investors fixate on the AI boom, a warning from a group of Wall Street bankers whose job is to help the U.S. government borrow went unnoticed.

In minutes released Aug. 5, the Treasury Borrowing Advisory Committee—a panel of senior bond dealers and investors, known as TBAC, that advises the Treasury on its own funding—warned that at current auction sizes, the government faces a $1.45 trillion funding shortfall in fiscal 2027–28.

What that means takes a primer to understand how Washington actually borrows. The Treasury doesn't take out one huge annual loan, rather, it raises cash by selling debt at regularly scheduled auctions. The shortest-dated IOUs, sometimes called "T-bills," come due in a year or less, while the longer-dated notes and bonds — known as "coupons" — run anywhere from two to 30 years.

The T-bills offer Washington, now, a rare opportunity to borrow money for the cheap.

At the time of writing, the three-month bill yielded around 3.8%, while the 10-year Treasury yield sat around 4.6%, and the 30-year at a multi-decade high above 5%. So what Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has done is lean unusually hard on the cheaper rate today to finance a roughly $2 trillion annual deficit. That holds down reported borrowing costs but leaves the government more exposed to inflation and rising rates.

The committee's own minutes hint at the strain: rising interest costs drove the biggest jump in Treasury outlays this year, up $120 billion. The government's total debt on interest alone now runs over $1 trillion annually, more than the United States spends on national defense.

That worries Jon Hilsenrath, the veteran Federal Reserve watcher who spent decades at The Wall Street Journal and now runs his own advisory firm, Serpa Pinto Advisory.

"If there are cracks that show up in the financial system over the next few years, I've been expecting them to show up in Treasury debt," he said in an interview. "If you look at any serious financial crisis, all you've got to do is follow the debt." In 2008, that meant mortgages, but today, he argues, "all the growth has been in federal debt."

The even bigger problem, Hilsenrath says, is a collision taking shape with the Treasury and the Fed. Just as Treasury is likely forced back toward longer-term bonds, the Fed under new Chair Kevin Warsh is moving to shrink its own balance sheet. The TBAC minutes note dealers expect the Fed's holdings to drift toward shorter maturities and more bills—and Hilsenrath says a Warsh-appointed new Fed committee, due to report on the balance sheet in December, will almost certainly conclude the Fed is overstocked on long-term Treasuries and must wind them down. So that would mean two waves of long-term supply, converging, with fewer buyers.

OpenAI will pause some work on an artificial intelligence model because of security concerns, the company stated Friday, following a series of incidents in which AI agents have escaped containment.

The company had evaluated the agent, Astra, and found “significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity”, which had moved to a “critical” threshold where it can find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, or devise and execute cyber-attacks when given only a “high level desired goal”.

OpenAI stated that the model was not involved in an incident in which one of its AI agents went rogue during a test, accessed the open web and hacked a startup, Hugging Face. The company discovered other instances in which autonomous agents had escaped containment, Reuters reported in July.

The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them. Still, critics of the AI industry have warned that such disclosures from OpenAI and its competitors Anthropic and Meta could be designed to generate hype about the technology’s power and thus spur additional interest from investors.

To prevent potential rogue behavior from AI agents, OpenAI is “implementing stricter security controls for higher-capability models and associated activities, including isolated testing environments, restricted network and tool access”, the company’s blog post stated. It will also install “enhanced model weight protections and encryption, additional monitoring and detection capabilities”.

The company will pause internal activities involving Astra that do not meet these new requirements.

“We’re committed to working alongside governments, safety institutes, and civil society to ensure that the frontier capabilities of models like Astra, and those that follow, are deployed responsibly and broadly for the benefit of all humanity,” the company stated.

Meta also disclosed this week that one of its models hacked another company during cybersecurity testing. And the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) announced on 4 August that agents powered by OpenAI and Anthropic had sent targeted emails to software developers in an attempt to pass a cyber challenge.

“These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world,” the institute stated in a blog post.

The organisation cautioned that the models’ sending of harmful software was not a case of a “model escaping its secure test environment” but rather that the group had intentionally permitted internet access to “best assess the maximum capability of models”.

Still, the “behaviour was possible, sustained, and new; that alone warrants attention”, AISI said.

The reports emerged while the Trump administration was finalizing a framework on how to test AI models for safety and cybersecurity risks. OpenAI and Anthropic, which have increased competition from China and other tech firms, have argued that open-source models, meaning those that allow anyone to see and modify the underlying program code, pose a security risk and pushed for additional federal regulations on them.
