fullText:
Observers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken over

When Sir Demis Hassabis said AI had brought the world to a “pivotal moment in human history” last month, he knew another big change was imminent.

This shift was closer to home. The Nobel prize-winning head of Google DeepMind, Google’s AI unit, announced this week he was relinquishing his day-to-day duties as chief executive and becoming chair. He is also taking on the role of chief scientist at DeepMind’s parent, Alphabet.

Hassabis and DeepMind have been key players in AI’s breakthrough era. The 50-year-old co-founded DeepMind and sold it to Google in 2014, which gave him the resources to oversee a number of advances.

These included building the AlphaGo system that mastered the Chinese board game Go and developing AlphaFold, a programme that predicts the 3D structure of proteins. The latter resulted in Hassabis being jointly awarded the 2024 Nobel prize in chemistry.

A former Google executive said the leadership overhaul showed London-based DeepMind being brought firmly into the orbit of its parent in Mountain View, California. DeepMind will now be run by Hassabis’s longstanding colleague, the US-based Koray Kavukcuoglu, who will take the non-CEO role of senior vice-president of DeepMind.

“The era of DeepMind as an independent actor is over and the obvious sign of that is you have gone from a charismatic founder-leader to appointing Koray in a non-CEO leadership role. Koray is a technical character, not an inspirational figure like Demis,” said the former executive.

The ex-Google employee added that it would be “galling” for Google and Hassabis that the latest iterations of Google’s flagship AI model series, Gemini, have lost ground to rival models developed by its US rivals Anthropic and OpenAI.

Hassabis has said he was looking forward to focusing more on the “big picture” for AI and believed he was handing over operational management of a unit that was well placed for the competitive battles ahead.

Internally, DeepMind is a workplace where there have been political tensions. Employees who spoke to the Guardian said there was internal disquiet over the company’s work with the Pentagon. Earlier this year, a former Google DeepMind employee launched a legal challenge against Google, claiming they were unfairly dismissed for their views on Gaza.

That employee was involved in unionisation efforts at Google DeepMind, which have taken place against a backdrop of concern that Google’s AI could assist militaries, including the Israel Defense Forces. Another Google DeepMind employee resigned from the company in mid-July, citing Google’s work with the Pentagon and the US Department of Homeland Security.

One said to the Guardian that Hassabis’s departure was the “end of an era”.

“Now the person we were supposed to trust to get the right outcomes for humanity has stepped away,” they said. Google DeepMind “has become just another subdivision of Google”, they added.

Rosa Curling, the executive director of Foxglove, a campaign group that supported the Google DeepMind employee in their legal challenge, said: “The departure of the co-founder of a company that once prided itself on its ethical credentials is likely to cause further concern among its frontier AI staff about how their work will end up being used in the real world.”

Google has said it is committed to the “private and public sector consensus” that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without “appropriate human oversight”. While Google has declined a voluntary union recognition agreement in London, it has said it valued “the constructive and direct dialogue that we have with our employees about building a positive and successful workplace”.

On the commercial side, a new cutting-edge model, Gemini 3.5 Pro, has yet to be released amid reports it has been delayed owing to attempts to improve its code-writing abilities – a core part of the appeal of Anthropic and OpenAI’s best products.

Google’s two AI labs, London-based DeepMind and California-based Google Brain, were merged into Google DeepMind under Hassabis’s leadership three years ago. Control now appears to be moving back to the US, where Google’s co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly playing a bigger role in AI development.

Citing the departure of the leading AI researcher Yann LeCun from Meta and Geoffrey Hinton from Google as another example of “the end of an era in the AI ecosystem”, the former executive added: “This is very clearly a sign that the science-driven agenda of leadership in these labs has given way to cold, hard commercial reality that all of these companies want to make a return on the hundreds of billions of dollars they have invested in AI.”

The source added, however, that Google still had the benefit of being able to combine its Gemini models with an impressive suite of products, from its all-conquering search product to its cloud platform and YouTube. Thanks to its search business it also has the money to continue investing heavily in AI, having generated net income – a US measure of profit – of $132bn (£98bn) last year.

Hassabis has also taken on a more statesman-like role in recent years. The reference to a “pivotal moment” came in a blogpost in which he called for a US safety body to assess cutting-edge models, with the hope it would lead to the establishment of global standards.

The need for such a body, Hassabis argued, was pressing because the tech industry was approaching the “pivotal” point of achieving AGI, the term for a theoretical state of AI where a system can perform any human cognitive task – which also means being capable of performing white collar jobs in sectors such as law, finance and health.

A Google spokesperson said: “This is a move Demis has been thinking about for a while. He is very excited, and this will give him more time to focus on AI-driven scientific breakthroughs.” They disputed that the changes had anything to do with the performance of Gemini.

Hassabis’s move was announced alongside the departure of Jeff Dean, a veteran Google engineer and DeepMind’s chief scientist, who is leaving along with three other top researchers to form an AI startup called Discovery Loop.

According to one former Google employee, Dean’s departure could augur further personnel losses. Dean’s move also follows OpenAI’s poaching in June of Google’s Noam Shazeer, a leading figure in the field as co-author of the 2017 research paper Attention is All You Need, a crucial step in developing chatbots.

“It’s hugely problematic for Google,” said Jeremy Nixon, a former AI researcher at Google and founder of Infinity Artificial Intelligence Institute, a startup. “It’s problematic because of who Jeff will hire and because the primary reason people want to work at Google is because of him and Noam Shazeer and all these other phenomenal researchers. It’s no longer true to say that if you want to work with the greatest researchers on the planet, you go to Google DeepMind.”

Nixon added that Dean was an “angelic diplomat” who could “deal with these complex political organisations”.

Google denies it faces a post-Dean talent crisis, pointing to attrition rates for AI talent for the first half of this year being lower than they were at this time last year.

If AI is indeed facing a pivotal moment, Google has just had one.

title: This man was secretly snapped by someone with smartglasses. He’s not alone in calling that a violation of privacy
description: The backlash to what some dub ‘pervert glasses’ is growing – but people living with disabilities point out the new tech can also be...
fullText:
The backlash to what some dub ‘pervert glasses’ is growing – but people living with disabilities point out the new tech can also be life-changing

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

One summer day earlier this year, Rhys left a cafe in Melbourne where he had been working remotely, when his phone pinged with a message on the dating app Grindr.

The message was a photo of him sitting at a table outside the cafe on his laptop, with his dog seated on the ground next to him. In the foreground, in a man’s hand was an iPhone unlocked.

The photo had been taken moments before with Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses, unbeknown to Rhys.

“He essentially wrote something about my dog being cute and apologised for not saying hi,” says Rhys, who asked that his surname not be used.

Rhys never noticed a flash, despite Meta Ray-Bans requiring an LED light to alert others to the device filming or taking pictures.

It felt creepy, Rhys says, particularly because the person didn’t say hi in the first place before surreptitiously taking a photo to send to him.

Smartglasses, such as Meta’s Ray-Bans, which have built-in cameras, microphones, and AI assistants, are growing in popularity as the clunky, ugly designs of earlier models are replaced with styles that are increasingly indistinguishable from regular glasses.

Meta says it has sold more than 7m of the glasses worldwide. It recruited the celebrity Kylie Jenner to star in online advertisements and partnered with social media influencers across the globe to attempt to bring the technology into the mainstream – and particularly into the hands of women.

Other companies like Snapchat are following with their own versions as tech companies look to find the next evolution beyond the smartphone.

But there is a growing backlash to, as they have been dubbed by some, “pervert glasses”. There are reports of women being filmed without their consent and having their interactions with a glasses-wearing influencer posted on social media. An ad by activist group Everyone Hates Elon features the late sex trafficker and paedophile Jeffrey Epstein wearing the glasses with the slogan “glasses for people who don’t do consent”.

While the price point remains high for the top-of-the-line models, cheaper versions are also becoming popular. Online retailers Amazon and Temu both sell knockoffs, while Australian low-cost retailer Kmart’s Anko-branded $89 camera glasses have already sold out, as Guardian Australia reported this week.

That news led to a petition by Australian activist group GetUp calling for a ban on the Anko glasses. As of Friday it had 21,000 signatures.

“It could be interpreted as a democratisation of access to these technologies,” Dr Fareed Kaviani, a research fellow in the Emerging Technologies Research Lab at Monash University, says of the Anko-branded glasses.

“But it’s not really a democratisation of consent – there’s a total lack of the ability for people to not only know if they’re being filmed … but there’s an inability to consent to being filmed.

“It really changes the dynamics of public space, raises a lot of privacy concerns, and a lot of concerns around the more vulnerable members of the public – especially children.”

Researchers at the University of Sydney analysed 350 publicly-available Instagram videos shot on smartglasses from around the world during 2023 to 2026, showing what they said was “a shift to discreet, point-of-view recording that is difficult for bystanders to detect”.

In a subset of these videos, around 60% of interactions could be classified as potential harassment, with subjects visibly uneasy or attempting to disengage, they say. In 43% of videos women were also abused in the comments of the post with some even revealing their personal details.

“Smart glasses have given pickup artists a new tool to further exploit women,” one of the researchers, Dr Joanne Gray, says in a statement accompanying the early findings on Friday. “You don’t know if you’re being filmed; that footage is then uploaded, exposing you to a wider web of harassment.”

But smartglasses do have some positive use cases. Graeme Innes, who has been blind since birth, says Meta’s Ray-Bans have been life-changing.

“I just use them all the time, and the fact they’re hands-free, it just makes a huge difference to my everyday life,” he says.

The former disability commissioner, now chancellor of Central Queensland University, says the glasses allow him to go for a walk and get feedback on his surroundings with the help of a visual description service.

At home, he can use it to check his credit card numbers, read a packet on an item in the kitchen cupboard, and to get cooking instructions.

“I was in a restaurant with my wife the other day, and I picked up the menu on the table, and just read it and chose what I want … that’s just something I’ve not been able to easily do in the past,” Innes says.

Chris Edwards, Vision Australia’s chief mission officer, says his life fundamentally changed when he got the Meta Ray-Bans two years ago, with the main benefit being the devices are hands-free, meaning he can use the AI assistant, or visual description services, to navigate.

“Getting support by humans is costly and impractical,” he says. “I do a lot of travelling for my work. And if I wanted to get similar support by a human, I would probably have to hire them for two hours.

“When I’m travelling [now] I can go to a location, put on my Meta glasses and be able to get descriptions of what’s around me, whether it’s a sign or a street sign or a bit about my location, all of those sorts of things.”

Specialist glasses for blind or low-vision people were available prior to the release of the current wave of smartglasses, but Edwards says they cost thousands of dollars and were not covered by the national disability insurance scheme.

Both Innes and Edwards acknowledge privacy concerns, but Innes says “that horse bolted 15 years ago when we got smartphones”.

“You can discreetly take pictures with a smartphone and the same privacy issues are there, so to single out the glasses as problematic – I don’t follow that logic,” he says.

Kaviani says the glasses are a “gamechanger” as an assistive technology, but “they’re not being marketed that way”.

Gray says governments should be acting early before the risks of the technology become “normalised and widespread”, and current privacy and harassment frameworks are not designed to address covert, continuous recording in public and semi-public spaces.

Meta last month rolled out an update that disables the camera if the LED light is interfered with, and also reportedly began removing videos from its platforms of wearers using the device to harass strangers in public.

However, legal recourse can be difficult. A new privacy tort in Australian federal law allows individuals to sue for invasion of privacy, but it is expensive for one person to take on.

If the images are posted to social media, they can be reported under eSafety’s adult cyber abuse scheme or children’s cyberbullying scheme. A spokesperson for eSafety says so far there have been a “small number of complaints where camera-enabled smart glasses may have been involved” and the regulator is closely monitoring how the technologies are being used.

“When it comes to filming people in public, just because technology makes something possible doesn’t necessarily mean it’s appropriate,” the spokesperson says.

The Australian privacy commissioner, Carly Kind, says smartglasses will “fundamentally alter our experience of interpersonal interactions”, and regulators should consider if new laws are required.

“As long as public trust in technology companies remains extremely low, the bar for establishing a social licence for rolling out new tech will be high,” Kind says.

title: The ornithological artist drawing 1,000 birds by hand – all for an app that wants you off your phone

fullText:
The mission of the Flock app is quietly subversive: to encourage users to ditch their screens and explore the wonderful world of birding

On a brilliantly bright afternoon in his gallery and studio in Bolinas, a small town on the northern California coast, Keith Hansen was putting the finishing touches on a watercolor of an almost improbably flamboyant painted bunting.

With an ultra-fine sable brush, he made a few intricate additions to the cobalt blue plumage on the bunting’s head, and, satisfied with his work, slipped the watercolor into a stout binder that every few days welcomes a new addition.

“That was number 420,” he said. Or to put it another way, just 584 to go.

Hansen, a renowned ornithological illustrator and author, has a monumental task – a hand-painted compendium of every one of the roughly 1,000 bird species ever recorded from the US and Canada, including those found in waters up to 200 miles from shore, Hawaiian birds not included. When finished, it will complete the visual backbone of an app called Flock, whose mission, compared with that of most apps, is quietly subversive.

For rather than seeking to monopolize and monetize its users’ attention, it deftly employs elements of computer gaming and social networking to draw people outward, into the world of birding, with the broader aim of cultivating a community of conservationists.

Flock was conceived and created by two of Hansen’s friends, Adam Donkin and Bob Stevenson. Both have impressive tech industry CVs. Donkin, 52, who lives not far from Hansen in Marin county’s San Geronimo valley, worked for many years as a product and user experience designer. As a lead product designer at Amazon, he led the charge on design for several models of the Kindle e-reader.

Stevenson, a 58-year-old Scotsman, lives in St Helena in the Napa valley. He founded his first company in Edinburgh at 18, and at 24, moved to California to work as an art director for Richard Branson’s Virgin Games, embarking on a decades-long career as an art or design director, or as a producer, for more than 50 video games.

Despite their disparate disciplines, the three friends are united by a shared passion for birds and birding.

Hansen fell in love with the avian world in sixth grade, when, on a walk in the Maryland woods, his brother, Rob, drew his attention to a cedar waxwing. “It’s just an exquisite bird,” Hansen recalled. He began illustrating birds during his senior year of high school, and in 1986 – after a decade and a half observing and studying birds on numerous expeditions – he settled in Bolinas, opening his gallery there in 1991.

Donkin grew up on the San Francisco peninsula and began birding at the age of four under the wing of his father’s friend Rich Stallcup, an esteemed ornithologist and birder, and a founder of the Point Reyes Bird Observatory. “He was like a nature wizard,” said Donkin. “Birds and animals would appear when you were in the field with him. He knew every bird by call and by sight.”

Donkin moved to Marin in 2012. “When I moved to Marin,” he said, “Rich introduced me to the thriving birding community here, including Keith.”

That same year, Stevenson was looking for a designer for his new company. “One of our investors recommended that we chat with this designer, Adam,” said Stevenson. “It was meant to be a quick call, but we ended up talking for over an hour. We became friends on the first call.”

In 2016, Donkin visited Stevenson at his home in the southern Marin town of Tiburon, overlooking Richardson Bay, a major habitat for migrating waterbirds. “One day Adam came round to the house,” Stevenson recalled. “I didn’t know that he was an avid birder. He turned up and said, ‘Hey, dude, you’ve got to bird! Do you have binoculars?’”

Stevenson, who had recently stepped away from his company to focus on his family, fell hard and fast for birding. He bought binoculars, scopes and cameras, began birding from his deck, and, as an outlet for his avian photography, opened his own gallery in Tiburon.

He was also struck by the ways in which birding resembled multi-player gaming, in that it involved learning new skills, a mastery curve, collecting (by way of so-called yard lists and life lists – tabulations of the bird species sighted in one’s yard, or over a lifetime), an awareness of how one is progressing relative to others, and a community which, while competitive, helps its members learn more quickly. He also recognized, at the age of 48, what he had given up by trading the beauty of the natural world for computer screens. “It was such a revelation, because going back to nature at that age, you realize what you’ve been missing.”

Shortly after, he and Donkin began discussing the idea of building an app around birding. For Donkin, his friend’s newfound passion was a catalyst. “I had the experience with Bob of turning someone on to it, and seeing what a huge impact it had on him.”

For Stevenson, the spark was a conversation with Robert Snow, the president of the Fresno Audubon Society, who said the organization was concerned about its ability to bring future generations into birding, as this was critical to perpetuating its mission of protecting birds and their habitats.

To Donkin, the path from birding to conservation is a natural progression. “Birding creates an infinite well of curiosity,” he said. “You start to notice things and think, ‘Well, how can I help?’ You might start with providing water, providing food, providing shelter. By restoring habitat in your area, you can have an impact. It could be your yard, a park in your neighborhood, sometimes ranch land, sometimes public land.”

Initially Stevenson and Donkin thought they might develop an app in partnership with Audubon, or with the Cornell Lab of Ornithology in Ithaca, New York, where they had given a presentation on the parallels between birding and gaming, with an eye towards how aspects of game design could be employed to increase engagement with the Cornell Lab’s Merlin app, which identifies birds based on their songs and calls, or images.

They ultimately decided to strike out on their own and, in 2017, set to work on Flock. Having worked on projects backed by publishers and by investors in Silicon Valley, Stevenson said they decided to fund it themselves “so we would not be bound by anyone’s rules”. They also set out to break the addictive conventions of app design. “The games industry is so comfortable making experiences that are so engaging that you can’t look away,” said Donkin, “and we were very aware of the negative aspects of social media.”

“We didn’t want to make something that got you addicted to the dopamine hit of getting a like, or followers,” Donkin continued. “We wanted to make something that was a companion to the experience of birding. In an attention-based economy, we’re going to use that same system, but we’re going to flip it. We’re not trying to get your attention on the app, we’re trying to get your attention away from your phone so that you can then turn your attention outward.”

The result is an app whose interface is refreshingly spare and minimalistic, with a tab where users can search for birds or for other users; another for recording sightings, made, perhaps with the aid of the Merlin app or an old-fashioned field guide; a leaderboard which ranks users according to the number of unique species they saw in the current month; and a community tab where users can upload photos, message one another, and congratulate other users on their sightings.

As with every detail of the app, even the way in which users cheer one another on was carefully considered. Instead of a “like” button, there is a “high-five” button. “We put ‘high five’ rather than ‘like’,” Stevenson explained, “because kids were using it, and we wanted it to be, ‘Nice job on seeing that bird!’ rather than, ‘I like you.’ We didn’t want kids to collect likes.”

They enlisted their longtime friend Hansen, whose artistic sensitivity brought a unique beauty to the app. While Stevenson coded, Donkin scanned and processed new batches of illustrations as Hansen completed them, following an algorithm that sorted the bird species in order from the most- to the least-commonly seen. Given that it can take Hansen up to four days to complete an illustration, this prioritized the birds Flock users are more likely to encounter: an American robin or a northern cardinal, for instance, rather than a Steller’s sea eagle, a huge Siberian raptor, one of which, acting on some unknown impulse in 2020, flew from northern Asia to Alaska and then Texas, before settling on the coast of Maine.

In early 2025, they released Flock on Apple’s app store. By April of that year, Flock had about 100 users. Today, although Donkin and Stevenson have not yet done anything in the way of marketing, it has on the order of 1,000. Among the recent enhancements they enjoy are uncannily realistic animations that bring Hansen’s illustrations to life. The short animations – which Stevenson created with AI, with Hansen’s guidance – give a sense of the way each particular bird moves. The formerly static white-crowned sparrow now darts its head this way and that in a most sparrow-like fashion, peering inquisitively at its viewer; the great blue heron, meanwhile, tiptoes along a sandy bank, and pausing, stealthily lowers its bill to the water’s surface, preparing to strike.

Among Flock’s growing flock is Amy Tan, the bestselling writer whose most recent work, The Backyard Bird Chronicles, grew from a series of pencil sketches, color portraits and journal notes she collected on her avian neighbors during the pandemic. A friend of Hansen’s for 10 years, and more recently of Stevenson’s, Tan logged her first sightings in the app late last summer. In an email, Tan wrote that Flock was “hands down the most beautiful bird app and the easiest one to track and share sightings of my backyard birds. With each bird I add to my daily list, I feel rewarded when its illustration suddenly comes to life. All my friends are blown away and become instant fans.”

This reporter, meanwhile, who entered his first sighting – a western gull – in Flock last spring, has found himself growing ever more attuned to the sights, sounds and habits of his feathered compatriots in San Francisco, and has recently begun shopping for a hummingbird feeder.

title: Rising number of UK children report seeing explicit deepfakes of themselves

fullText:
Exclusive: anonymous flagging service says cases have surged, as watchdog says AI is making sexualised or ‘nudified’ content easier to produce

Children in the UK have reported a surge in explicit deepfake images featuring their likenesses, as a safety watchdog warned AI is making such content easier to produce.

The Report Remove service, which blocks intimate images from appearing online, said there had been a rapid increase in imagery that had been digitally manipulated or “faked” in some way, including with AI and nudification tools.

In the first six months of this year it received 420 reports from children of images of themselves that they believed had been faked or manipulated to appear explicit. The number has already exceeded its 2025 total of 397.

Dan Sexton, chief technology officer at the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF), which operates Report Remove alongside the NSPCC children’s charity, said the figures underscored the difficulty of preventing online images from being manipulated in an age of widely available and capable AI tools.

“If someone can take a benign image of a child from the internet and create child sexual abuse material with it, there is nothing that child can do to stop it from happening apart from preventing anyone from taking pictures of them – or not putting pictures of themselves online,” he said.

Report Remove has received so many reports of manipulated images from under-18s in recent years that it has added a check box to its online submission form allowing them to flag the material as deepfaked.

Sexton said the figures confirmed a fear that AI would improve in capability and be used to manipulate images of real people.

“This is one of the harms we were worried about when we first saw AI image generators being used, that they would be used to create child sexual abuse material featuring real children,” he said.

“Everyone in the world is at risk,” Sexton added.

The IWF, which monitors the distribution of child sexual abuse material [CSAM] online, said the majority of the reports of manipulated images made to Report Remove in 2025 and 2026 were so severe that they passed the CSAM threshold. AI-generated CSAM is illegal in the UK and the government has made it illegal to adapt an AI model to create abuse material or to distribute such models to others.

Rani Govender, an online safety expert at the NSPCC, said tech companies must put stronger safety protections in their AI products to prevent the creation of explicit material.

“This rise in children reaching out because fake or AI‑generated sexual images have been created of them is alarming but also sadly predictable,” she said. “Tech companies cannot keep pushing out AI products without embedding strong protections that prevent this material from being created in the first place.”

Sexton said some victims who had contacted Report Remove about manipulated images had been targeted for sextortion, where a blackmailer threatens to publish the material unless they receive financial payment or demands more explicit images from the victim.

Report Remove is a service that allows children to anonymously flag intimate images or videos of themselves that have been sent to former partners, sextortion fraudsters or could appear online. The service turns those images into a “hash”, or digital fingerprint, which is shared with major tech platforms, which can take the image down or prevent it from being uploaded.

The rise of AI-enabled deepfakes has prompted a series of warnings about posting identifiable pictures of children online.

Last month the National Crime Agency and IWF encouraged parents and guardians to keep pictures of their children away from public display online. They suggested making social media accounts private or sharing pictures of children through a “close friends” group only.

The guidance also followed cases in which cybercriminals had attempted to blackmail schools by scraping pictures of children, using AI to convert them into child sexual abuse material, then threatening to publish the imagery. Schools have been urged to remove identifiable pictures of pupils’ faces from their websites and social media accounts.

title: Pritchard eyes world title defence after Euro win
description: The 34-year-old from Mumbles, near Swansea will head to Amsterdam having overcome a freak pre-Europeans injury to retain his title in Italy.
fullText:
Welsh Para-rower Ben Pritchard hopes his successful European title defence can be the springboard to retaining his world title later this month.

The 34-year-old will head to Amsterdam having overcome a freak pre-event injury to beat Italian Giacomo Perini in the PR1 men's single sculls at the European Rowing Championships in Varese, Italy last weekend.

"When I landed in Italy, there was a malfunction on the hoist that got me on to the coach and the cable snapped, so it dropped me from the top of the hoist to the bottom, which obviously causes a bit of an injury, which I was managing throughout the championships," Pritchard told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast.

Pritchard, from Mumbles, Swansea, added: "I actually thought I may not have come out on top given the injury that I was coping with, but I'm glad I did. It was a great race though.

"It's probably one of the best races we've had in in a couple of years because it was neck and neck until the last 250m."

Pritchard named BBC Wales Sports Personality of the Year 2025

Pritchard, the BBC Cymru Wales Sports Personality of the Year for 2025, and his Great Britain team-mates have stayed at Varese to complete their preparations for the World Rowing Championships, that take place from 24-30 August at Amsterdam's Bosbaan venue.

"I always feel that this this camp is where we get the most speed," said Pritchard.

"We do a load of speed work in this last block now for the world championships, so I'm hoping that that'll set me in good stead for the future.

"I have just seen my competitor Erik Horrie from Australia training this morning, and he looks really fast as well. So hopefully we can get a good race but it's an outdoor sport - anything could happen.

"But it's going to be nice to be out on the Bosbaan in Amsterdam because the Welsh men's hockey team and ladies' team have got their World champs as well, so I'm going to hopefully get across and watch some of their games too."

Pritchard is one of Para-rowing's dominant forces. Since winning gold at the 2024 Paralympics he has set multiple world records in his event and added the 2025 European and world crowns to his tally.

He says he went to Italy with added desire to succeed after his Swansea coach Andrew Williams lost his father.

"It was a big one and an emotional one, but gave you the actual motivation when the going got tough in the race, that's for sure," he said.

However, Pritchard was comfortable facing and beating Perini on his home waters, saying: "I think it's more my home water than his.

"You know, we're in his home country, but as a team, we come here twice a year to train and spend two weeks of time here, so I've been coming here now for nine years.

"It feels like a home to me, and the club members know me and all that kind of stuff, so I feel that actually I had a good share of the support in the stands."

title: Why is the EFL Cup being played on a weekend?
description: The bulk of the EFL cup's first round fixtures will take place on a weekend, despite traditionally being a midweek cup competition.
fullText:
The first round of the 2026-27 EFL Cup campaign began on Thursday, 6 August 2026.

Of the 35 first-round ties, 34 will be played between Friday and Monday this weekend.

The competition, known as the Carabao Cup due to the tournament's sponsors, is traditionally played in midweek. The only usual exception is the final, which is played at Wembley on a Sunday.

The competition normally begins on a midweek date following the opening round of Championship, League One and League Two fixtures.

But this season, the competition will instead start on the weekend prior to the start of the EFL league seasons.

Following consultation with clubs from the EFL over a proposed schedule, it was agreed the EFL Cup's first round will take place a week prior to the season starting.

Originally, the competition had been due to fully start on Friday, 7 August. However, Bristol City's first-round match against Walsall on Thursday, 6 August meant the full competition started a day earlier.

The move to have the competition starting a week before the league season allows more of a rest period for players compared to other seasons, where teams can end up playing three times in quick succession due to the opening round being sandwiched in between two league fixtures.

Some weekend fixtures took place in 2020 and 2021, as well as 14 games in 2012. However, there has been no full round of weekend fixtures, excluding the final, this century.

The first round will only include Championship, League One and League Two teams, with Premier League clubs starting to enter from the second round onward.

title: Chapman could return to UK next week after brain bleed
description: British boxer Raven Chapman could fly back to the UK next week after undergoing a second successful surgery on a brain bleed she suffered following a sparring session in Denmark.
fullText:
Britain's Raven Chapman could travel back to the UK next week after undergoing a second successful surgery on a brain bleed she suffered following a sparring session in Denmark.

The 32-year-old former world title challenger collapsed after training on 24 July and was taken by helicopter to hospital, where she was diagnosed with a brain haematoma and cerebral oedema.

After undergoing emergency surgery and being placed in a medically induced coma, Chapman's management company, Vote Boxing, said she has had another successful procedure.

"This marks another important step in her recovery while also making it safer for her to travel back to the UK," a statement said.

"If everything continues to progress as hoped, we are aiming for Raven to fly home sometime next week, where she can continue her recovery surrounded by her family and loved ones.

"Although there is still a long road ahead, this is a significant milestone, and we remain hopeful as Raven continues to make progress each day."

Chapman has won 10 professional fights with two losses.

The Norwich-born fighter lost to Skye Nicolson for the WBC featherweight title in October 2024 in the only women's world-title fight ever held in Saudi Arabia.

A GoFundMe page has been launched to help raise funds for Chapman's rehabilitation and after-care has raised over £88,000.

"We would also like to take this opportunity to sincerely thank everyone who has supported Raven through her GoFundMe, as well as everyone who has sent messages, shared their prayers, and shown kindness throughout this incredibly difficult time," the statement added.

"Your generosity and support have meant more than words can express and have provided tremendous strength to Raven and her loved ones.

"Thank you for continuing to keep Raven in your thoughts as she continues her recovery."

title: Fijian Vunilagi dies in Japan from suspected heatstroke after training
description: Fijian Saimoni Vunilagi has died of suspected heatstroke after a training session, his Japanese club Kyuden Voltex announce.
fullText:
Fijian Saimoni Vunilagi has died of suspected heatstroke after a training session, his club Kyuden Voltex have announced.

The Japanese second division team, based in Fukuoka, said the 26-year-old was taken to hospital and died on Friday, 7 August.

Temperatures in the southern city of Fukuoka this week have reached 35C degrees.

"After team practice on Monday, 3 August 2026, Saimoni displayed symptoms consistent with severe heatstroke. He was transported to a medical facility for treatment, but despite the best efforts of the medical team, he sadly passed away," a team statement said.

"The players, staff, and all team associates are devastated by this sudden news.

"Although Saimoni had only recently joined Kyushu KV, his generous spirit and powerful style of play had raised high hopes for his contributions in the upcoming season.

"We humbly pray for the repose of his soul and extend our heartfelt condolences to his bereaved family.

title: NBA forward Clarke's death due to effects of drugs
description: Memphis Grizzlies forward Brandon Clarke's death was due to the effects of heroin and cocaine, the Los Angeles medical authority reveals.
fullText:
Memphis Grizzlies forward Brandon Clarke's death in May was caused by the "effects of heroin and cocaine", the Los Angeles authorities have revealed.

The County of Los Angeles Department of Medical Examiner ruled that the death was accidental., external

The 29-year-old was found unresponsive in a bedroom at a house in San Fernando Valley on 11 May, 2026 and was pronounced dead by paramedics.

The medical examiner's office also listed the "combined effects of multiple prescription medications" as a "significant" contributor to his death but did not state what the medications were.

The medical examiner added that its full report would be available at a later date.

The Canada-born player was a first-round draft pick in 2019 but played only two games in the 2025-26 season because of injuries.

Paying tribute at the time, the Grizzlies said they were "heartbroken" by the loss, adding he was an "outstanding team-mate and an even better person whose impact on the organisation and the greater Memphis community will not be forgotten".

Clarke played 309 NBA games, including 50 starts, and scored an average of 10.2 points per game.

A month prior to his death, Clarke was arrested in Arkansas on charges that included speeding and possession of a controlled substance.

Clarke was born in Vancouver and was a dual citizen of Canada and the USA.

After playing college basketball at San Jose State and then Gonzaga, he was drafted by the Oklahoma City Thunder and traded to the Grizzlies soon after.

title: Arsenal sign Guimaraes from Newcastle in £75m deal
description: Premier League champions Arsenal sign Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United for £75m.
fullText:
Arsenal have signed Bruno Guimaraes from Newcastle United for £75m.

The former Newcastle captain made it clear he wanted to join the Premier League champions earlier this summer.

The 28-year-old Brazil midfielder, who has signed a four-year deal with the option of a further 12 months, called the move one of the "toughest decisions" of his life.

"This move is very tough because Newcastle means so much to me," he added.

"But I wanted to experience something new in my life. I feel ready for a new challenge for myself and my family."

Newcastle said they wished Guimaraes and his family well.

Guimaraes left Newcastle's training camp in La Manga in Spain earlier this week to finalise his move to Emirates Stadium following a breakthrough in talks.

He revealed he received messages from a number of his future team-mates, including countryman Gabriel as well as fellow midfielder Declan Rice.

Following their previous battles in the middle of the park, Rice told him "come here and please no more fights, now we're friends".

"I'm at the point of my life, I think I need a challenge like this," Guimaraes said.

"I want to win trophies, I want to make history and I think I'm in the right place to do it. I'm so excited to start."

Guimaraes joined a Newcastle side in relegation trouble in January 2022 and went on to play a crucial role in their improvement in fortunes under former head coach Eddie Howe.

The Brazilian became the first captain in seven decades to lift a major domestic trophy for Newcastle after they defeated Liverpool in the 2025 EFL Cup final.

He was also part of the side who qualified for the Champions League in 2023 and 2025, before they slipped to 12th place in the Premier League last season.

title: Goals galore - the wildest scores in EFL Cup history
description: BBC Sport looks at some of the wildest games - and scorelines - the EFL Cup has produced as the competition returns for a new season.
fullText:
Some clubs use the early rounds to give experience to young players, shake off the last of their pre‑season rust and perhaps sneak an early season upset, but that can also result in some staggering scorelines.

From 12‑goal thrillers to 10-0 humiliations and penalty shootouts that threaten to last almost as long as the match itself, the EFL Cup has had it all over the years.

Here's a look at the some of the most wild games the competition has ever produced...

Round one, 13 August 2014, Victoria Road

Let's start off with a bang and talk about the joint-highest scoring EFL Cup tie in history.

The tie between Dagenham & Redbridge, then in League Two, and a Brentford side recently promoted to the Championship may not have looked the most interesting on paper, but it certainly delivered a gripping match.

A remarkable match was level at 4-4 after 90 minutes and the goals kept coming in extra-time.

The Daggers took the lead for the first time in the 113th minute and looked set to progress as they led 6-5 late on, before Brentford's Harlee Dean scored in the 117th minute to take the match to penalties.

After Jack Connors and Ashley Chambers missed for Dagenham, skipper Kevin O'Connor stepped up to score the winning spot-kick for Brentford.

Round two, 20 September 2005, Adams Park

Aston Villa manager David O'Leary admitted his side were "on the verge" of being part of a cup shock when they faced Wycombe Wanderers in 2005.

But having trailed the League Two side 3-1 at half-time, Villa responded with seven goals in the second half to secure the win.

Some Villa fans reacted angrily when goals from Nathan Tyson, Roger Johnson and Tommy Mooney put Wycombe in a strong position at the halfway stage.

But goals from Milan Baros and James Milner made it 3-3, before a Craig Easton own goal, two from Gareth Barry and further strikes from Milner and Steven Davis completed an emphatic turnaround.

Second round, second leg, 25 October 1983, Boleyn Ground

We're going back to the days when the early rounds had two legs, the tournament was called the Milk Cup, and the day West Ham United recorded their record win.

There was little warning that an eye‑catching scoreline was coming, given John Lyall's Division One leaders had only edged the first‑leg tie 2-1 at Fourth Division Bury.

But West Ham raced to a 5-0 half‑time lead, with Alvin Martin, Trevor Brooking and Tony Cottee tearing Bury apart.

Cottee completed his hat‑trick before the break and the Hammers were just as ruthless in the second half.

Cottee added his fourth, Alan Devonshire got another, Ray Stewart buried a penalty, and Brooking tapped in late on as West Ham reached double figures.

Fourth round, 30 October 2012, Madejski Stadium

An incredible match, the joint-highest scoring EFL Cup tie in history, and it took extra-time to find a winner.

Still without a win in their return to the Premier League, Reading threw away any joy their fans were feeling as they led Arsenal 4-0 by capitulating to lose 7-5.

Arsenal found themselves four down after 35 minutes, but Theo Walcott's goal before half‑time sparked a comeback that dragged the match into extra-time.

Marouane Chamakh put Arsenal in front for the first time on the night with a goal in the first period of extra-time, only for Reading striker Pavel Pogrebnyak to make it 5-5.

But Walcott restored Arsenal's lead before Chamakh completed the scoring.

A remarkable night was further added to by the faintly ridiculous moment when Olivier Giroud and Francis Coquelin threw their shirts into the crowd, thinking the match was over, only to have to awkwardly ask for them back once they realised extra‑time was still to come.

Semi-final first leg, 9 January 2019, Etihad Stadium

Burton Albion's first major semi‑final was somewhat ruined as they were roundly thrashed by Manchester City.

The 3,000 Brewers fans had to battle some M6 chaos just to get there and some might have wished they'd stayed stuck in traffic.

Nigel Clough's side had beaten a mixture of Premier League and Championship sides to get to the last four but were powerless to stop a rampant City side.

Gabriel Jesus scored four, with Kevin de Bruyne, Oleksandr Zinchenko, Phil Foden, Kyle Walker and Riyad Mahrez also scoring against the beleaguered League One side.

After Burton's fairy tale cup run finally ended, Clough said that Pep Guardiola invited him in for a glass of wine and quipped he hoped the Spaniard had "more than a glass."

The second leg finished 1-0 at the Pirelli Stadium, sealing a 10–0 aggregate victory for City.

Second round first leg, 23 September 1986, Anfield

League champions Liverpool showed their class with a 10-goal demolition of Fulham.

Steve McMahon scored four and missed a penalty as the Third Division side were swept aside at Anfield.

Ian Rush and John Wark struck early, Ronnie Whelan added a third, and McMahon scored either side of Wark's second.

He hit the bar from the spot before making it seven, with further goals from Rush, McMahon and Nicol sealing the club's biggest victory in domestic competition.

Liverpool then won the second leg 3-2, advancing 13-2 on aggregate.

Third round, 17 September 2024, Deepdale

Yes, 1-1 isn't the most memorable scoreline, but the third-round tie between Preston North End and Fulham in 2024 makes it into the record books after producing the longest penalty shootout in the competition's history.

A total of 34 spot kicks were taken – 31 of which were successfully converted – as Paul Heckingbottom's men booked their place in round four.

Just when it seemed the shootout may never end, Fulham's Timothy Castagne blazed his spot-kick over the bar and Preston midfielder Ryan Ledson – who scored the game's opener in the 36th minute – fired in the decisive penalty.

The shootout eclipsed the previous record set in 2016 when Derby County beat Carlisle United 14-13 on penalties.

title: Red Sox reactions: Win streak hits nine straight in rout over Athletics
description: The Red Sox stretched their winning streak to nine games with a one-sided victory at home.
fullText:
BOSTON — Instant reactions from the Red Sox' win over the Athletics at Fenway Park Friday night:

1) The juggernaut continued to roll Friday night at Fenway as the Red Sox stomped the Athletics 13-1 to stretch their winning streak to nine games in a row. The Red Sox have now won — deep breath — 11 of their last 12, 27 of their last 30 and 35 of their last 43. The win also enabled them to pull even at home (29-29) as the team won for the 12th time at Fenway in the last 14 tries. The win was fueled by a strong performance from Payton Tolle (six innings of one-run ball) and supported by a 15-hit attack. The win marked the first time the Sox had scored 12 runs or 

2) How good was Payton Tolle Friday night? Put it this way: when you're being mentioned in the same sentence as Roger Clemens, that signifies a big night. Tolle's 14 strikeouts were the most for a Red Sox pitcher 23 or younger since Clemens fanned 20 Seattle Mariners on April 19, 1986. He also had the highest number of swing-and-misses (24) since James Paxton had 25 in June of 2023. Tolle was simply overpowering, striking out every member of the Athletics' starting lineup at least once except for outfielder Lawrence Butler. In five of his six innings, he posted multiple strikeouts. As impressive, perhaps, he didn't walk a single hitter.

3) Is Anthony Seigler busting out of his slump? After serving as a spark plug in the Red Sox' 15-game winning streak last month, Seigler went into a lengthy funk, to the point where he was hitting just .172 over a 20-game span, collecting just 11 hits in 64 at-bats, costing him playing time at second as Nick Sogard claimed the position. But Seigler had a two-hit game in the Sox' comeback win Thursday and he added a double and a single in the Friday romp. The last time Seigler had back-to-back games with multiple hits was June 24-25.

4) The Jarren Duran power show continues. Duran got the Red Sox on the board in the second inning when, after a one-out walk to Andruw Monasterio, Duran walloped a pitch into the Monster Seats. It was his third homer in the last five games, giving him 16 for the season. Recall that Duran erupted for nine homers in the month of May before cooling in a big way a month later. Is this the start of another big month for him at the plate? He's already tied his home run output from a year ago and is within five of his career high of 21, set in 2024.

5) Catcher Jake Rogers probably isn't going to be here for a long time. He was part of the Adley Rutschman trade because, after including Carlos Narváez in the deal, the Red Sox needed a veteran catcher to serve as a backup until Rutschman is cleared to play. But in a short span, Rogers has made his presence felt. In Thursday's marathon win, he worked a walk and had a sacrifice fly. On Friday, he belted Wall-ball doubles in each of his first two plate appearances, knocking in a run and scoring another.

6) The energy that Payton Tolle gives off is palpable. When center fielder Ceddanne Rafaela robbed Athletics second baseman Jonathan Ornelas for the final out in the third inning, Tolle celebrated with an exaggerated leg kick as he jumped off the mound. The big lefty isn't just good, he's highly entertaining and engaging.

7) It's likely that Raymond Burgos will have a very short stay with the Red Sox. Called up from Worcester to fortify a depleted bullpen after the 13-inning affair the night before, Burgos made the second major-league appearance of his career and contributed three shutout innings in relief of Tolle, retiring all nine hitters he faced.

8) In the middle game of the three-game set between the teams on Saturday, it will be a pitching matchup of LHP Jake Bennett (7-4, 2.90 ERA) vs. LHP Gage Jump (4-7, 4.59) at 4:10 p.m.

title: Rising 2028 OL prospect Ty Westenberger talks Utah offer
description: Standing 6-foot-5, the San Marcos standout discusses his rapid rise, a personal connection with Jordan Gross, and how the Utes' culture placed them among his early favorites.
fullText:
The Utah Utes have made an early impression on one of Southern California's rising offensive line prospects.

2028 offensive tackle Ty Westenberger, a 6-foot-5.5, 300-pound prospect out of San Marcos High School, is still early in his football journey. Despite only beginning the sport as a freshman, Westenberger has already picked up Power Four offers from both Utah and Cal as his recruitment continues to gain momentum.

For Westenberger, the offer was about more than football.

"The coaches spent a lot of time asking about my goals, family, football, and how I think about things like working out, nutrition, and other topics," Westenberger told me. "They talked about how they view me as a player and what they like about my game."

Then Jordan Gross made it official.

"When Coach Gross offered me, I was honestly shocked," he said. "My jaw dropped. I felt really grateful that a program like Utah believed in me and saw the potential for me to contribute there someday."

That relationship with Gross has only continued to grow.

"Coach Gross has been great throughout the recruiting process," Westenberger said. "He checks in regularly, I feel like he takes the time to get to know me, he's even reached out to my family."

"He is just so nice and seems so supportive. I've really liked building a relationship with him and learning more about his experience and the Utah program."

That relationship is a major reason Utah has positioned itself well early on.

"Utah is definitely one of the schools standing out to me right now," Westenberger said. "The way Coach Gross and the entire staff have treated me when I came to camp, along with the culture and atmosphere of the program, has made a strong impression on me."

As his recruitment continues, Westenberger said development will ultimately be one of the biggest factors in his decision.

"The biggest factors for me will be finding a school where I can be successful academically and develop as a football player," he said. "I want to go to a school with a strong football culture, great coaches, and a team that feels like family."

For now, though, his focus is on his junior season.

After undergoing shoulder surgery in January, Westenberger turned the setback into motivation.

"I had shoulder surgery in January, and I was afraid I was going to fall behind," he said. "But it actually motivated me to work even harder."

He also began training with a new coach, focusing on improving his footwork, technique and consistency.

"Since I only started playing football as a freshman, I feel like I had a lot of room to develop," Westenberger said. "I'm excited to show coaches how much my game has evolved since last season."

With two more years of high school football ahead of him, Westenberger's recruitment is still in the early stages.

But Utah got involved early, Jordan Gross has built a strong relationship, and the Utes have already put themselves in a good position with one of the West Coast's rising offensive line prospects.

fullText:
The WNBA may feature two former NBA first-round picks in the league next season.

The WNBA is currently at the center of a major debate around the potential inclusion of transgender athletes in the W. As expected, the majority is against that notion.

However, some players and coaches have openly supported the idea of trans athletes in the league. Keeping that in mind, former NBA player Enes Kanter Freedom recently declared for the 2027 WNBA Draft.

While fans were still taking in the Kanter news, another former NBA player has announced his interest in the 2027 WNBA Draft.

White made an exclusive appearance on Fox News to express his interest and desire to become a WNBA player.

"I'm transgender. I'm a woman. I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purpose of basketball, professional basketball, so I'll be declaring for the WNBA draft in 2027 as well," White said.

"I think I'd be unstoppable. But I'm a team-first guy. I'm a pass-first kind of player. I do the little things. I led my team in all five major stat categories at Iowa State University, so I do a little bit of everything.

"I'll do whatever the coach needs me to do. I'll do whatever the girls need me to do… I think it's only fair," White continued.

Although White featured in just three NBA games during his career, let's not forget that he is 6'8″, 270lbs and was a top-15 pick during the 2012 draft.

White then directly challenged the WNBA and urged them to release a statement against his declaration.

"I think the WNBA could come out and make a definitive statement about guys with a pair of balls playing in the Women's Association," White added.

But what if the WNBA ignores his declaration without a definitive statement? The 35-year-old is ready to pursue a legal route.

"Oh, no, I'm declaring. And I don't want to be discriminated against. I want fair treatment. I'm a young Black, hopefully United States Senator that would like a fair chance to participate as a sometimes-identifying-as-a-transgender-woman athlete," he said.

White concluded, stating, "I have to file a discrimination lawsuit, right? I mean, that's, that's ridiculous," he said. "We're gonna have to have a huge legal battle about discrimination if I can't play."

With White and Kanter's recent declarations, this puts the ball in the WNBA's court, as the league needs to put out a clear set of rules before the situation gets out of hand.

title: “It’s Gonna Be Me”: LeBron James’ Ex-Teammate Attempts to Spoil Kevin Love’s Reunion Desire With Public Demand to 76ers
description: We thought LeBron James’ announcement would end the tension of free agency. But the Philadelphia 76ers’ seismic offseason, anchored by the blockbuster acquisition of Jaylen Brown, has turned the franchise into the league’s top destination for ring-chasing veterans.
fullText:
We thought LeBron James' announcement would end the tension of free agency. But the Philadelphia 76ers' seismic offseason, anchored by the blockbuster acquisition of Jaylen Brown, has turned the franchise into the league's top destination for ring-chasing veterans. Kevin Love wants to ride off into the sunset after a potential reunion with his former Cleveland Cavaliers championship teammate.

While that puts his situation with the Utah Jazz into perspective, his dream has hit an unexpected snag. Philadelphia native and 14-year NBA veteran Markieff Morris has publicly thrown his hat in the ring, demanding that the Sixers prioritize homegrown talent among LeBron's former teammates.

When NBA insider Evan Sidery shared the report outlining Love's desire to land in Philadelphia, Morris took to social media to stake his own claim to the franchise's final roster opening. Responding directly to the speculation, the former 2020 Lakers champion tweeted:

"Shiddd if it's anybody getting that last Vet roster spot it's gonna be me! Philly raised!!!"

Get the Essentially Dunk Newsletter. League-wide coverage every day on the All-Stars, MVPs, iconic legends, and the drama defining the NBA.

The thing is, the 'last vet roster spot' isn't exactly vacant. ESPN's Dave McMenamin reported that Love's agent, Jeff Schwartz of Excel Sports Management, has been in contact with the 76ers' front office ever since LeBron finalized his decision to join Philadelphia. But the Sixers have 14 of their 15 roster spots filled, and they are tight on cap space.

Love, who spent last season with the rebuilding Utah Jazz, averaging 6.7 points and 5.8 rebounds in a limited role, reportedly harbors a strong interest in teaming up with James once more to chase another title before retirement.

Morris, a 6'9″ forward who turns 37 in September, brings deep local ties to the equation. Born and raised in Philadelphia alongside his twin brother, fellow NBA veteran Marcus Morris, Markieff's potential signing would mark a full-circle homecoming story.

Having spent 14 seasons across eight franchises, including championship experience alongside James during their 2020 Los Angeles Lakers title run, Morris represents a rugged, culture-setting presence eager to suit up for his hometown crowd. But unlike Love, he hasn't played in an NBA game since April 2025.

However, landing either veteran poses a logistical challenge for the 76ers. Philadelphia would have to waive or trade a player to accommodate an early-season signing. They're already operating near the hard cap of the first apron, making an immediate signing difficult.

Reports suggest that while Love remains intrigued by Philadelphia, he also maintains a strong relationship with Jazz head coach Will Hardy, leaving a return to Utah on the table if a buyout or roster spot opens up.

Alternatively, the Sixers could wait until mid-December to sign Love or Morris to a prorated veteran minimum contract without making an immediate trade.

With both Philadelphia and Utah operating at full roster capacity, any addition requires careful consideration, regardless of lobbying by these veteran contenders for a position.

Besides, the 76ers already have a loaded roster with James, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey, Brown, VJ Edgecombe, Kentavious Caldwell-Pope, and backups.

But the battle for the final seat on the bench has officially begun, with Morris making it abundantly clear that he intends to keep that spot in Brotherly Love.

title: ‘Can You Man Up’ – Belinda Bencic Lashes Out at Her Husband and Coaching Team During Tense Toronto Battle

fullText:
Belinda Bencic found herself locked in a closely contested battle with Taylor Townsend in the third round of the Canadian Open, narrowly avoiding an upset at the hands of the American.

Bencic's emotions came to the fore during the tense contest as she voiced her frustrations toward her coaching team in her player's box, which included her husband and fitness coach, Martin Hromkovič.

No. 12 seed Bencic made a strong start to her campaign at the WTA 1000 event in Toronto by securing a dominant 6-3, 6-1 win over Sloane Stephens in her opening match, following a first-round bye.

The 29-year-old faced a much tougher test in her third-round showdown with Taylor Townsend. Although Bencic fended off three set points in the opening set, Townsend edged her out in the tiebreak. Nevertheless, the Swiss fought back to clinch the second-set tiebreak and force a decider.

Despite winning the set, Bencic appeared unimpressed with her coaching team's demeanor in her player's box, lashing out in an animated outburst during the changeover.

"Can you man up and be loud? You! Yes," she said. "Shut up."

However, Bencic regained her composure when she took the court for the third set and eventually sealed a 6-7(5), 7-6(4), 6-4 victory after a grueling three-hour, 26-minute marathon.

On a personal level, Bencic not only has her husband by her side in Toronto but also their two-year-old daughter, Bella. During a press conference after her second-round win, the 29-year-old credited the Canadian Open for making their stay more convenient while traveling with a toddler.

"She's here with us, and the tournament is very nice. They said that they would provide an extra room paid for the moms that are traveling with the kids, so you have a bit more space for your team and all your luggage and everything. It's really nice from the tournament," Bencic said.

"I, in general, think the tournaments are getting so much better at helping with this and that. Sometimes they have like a kids' corner or like some toys or some area to play," she added.

title: Red Sox’ Jarren Duran starting to turn the power on again
description: Jarren Duran had a red-hot month of May with nine homers and already in August, he's hit three home runs.
fullText:
BOSTON — In the month of May, Red Sox outfielder Jarren Duran smacked nine homers.

Three months later, he appears to be heating up again when it comes to the long ball. Duran homered in the second inning of the Red Sox' 13-1 wipeout of the Athletics. The homer was his third in the last five games since the calendar flipped to August.

"Just putting good swings on the ball, trusting my process," said Duran, "and trusting my plan at the plate and it's just been working for me. Honestly, it's just about trusting myself and trying my approach at the plate and not skewing from it. That's kind of something that I struggle with a lot — I get too anxious and I don't trust my process and it shows when I start to chase and stuff."

Duran's homer was hit into the Monster Seats, and his ability to hit the ball hard the other way is generally a good indicator that he's on a good run.

"I'd like to say that the game is that easy, that I can guide the ball that way," said Duran. "But it happens when my swing's in a good place and the pitch takes me that way then I just go with it. It's not like force or anything like that; these guys are throwing too hard and (throwing) too many good pitches to be able to force it that way. But when I'm in a good spot and the balls are out there, the ball goes that way."

His recent spate of homers is part of a larger upturn at the plate. He's hitting .302 with an OPS of .830 over the last 14 games.

Now that he's hitting the ball out of the ballpark, his bat helps deepen the Red Sox' batting order in the bottom third of the lineup.

"He's in a good rhythm right now," said interim manager Chad Tracy, "and he's seeing the ball well and putting good swings on it. I've said, when he gets on a (hot streak), he can usually sustain for a bit. As far as the quality of contact and consistently squaring up the ball, it feels like (what he was doing in May). It's been over a week now that he's been taking really, really quality at-bats.

"He's hitting seventh. We've been swinging the bat great as a team for quite a while now, but when Jarren's going and you have someone down in the lower third who's not only getting on base but also has the slug, yeah, it makes us more dynamic."

title: “Winning Without Her”: Sue Bird Makes Bold Napheesa Collier Claim Amid Free Agency Implications Surrounding the Lynx Star
description: For a team that entered the 2026 season without its franchise star, the Minnesota Lynx have surprised fans. With her contract set to expire after the end of this season, Napheesa Collier missed 27 games after undergoing her second ankle surgery on March 24.
fullText:
For a team that entered the 2026 season without its franchise star, the Minnesota Lynx have surprised fans. With her contract set to expire after the end of this season, Napheesa Collier missed 27 games after undergoing her second ankle surgery on March 24. Yet the Lynx have risen to the top of the standings. Now that their star forward is back, Sue Bird has claimed that they've not only learned how to win without her, but have thrived.

"Napheesa Collier is back. She had offseason surgery on both ankles. Made her return just before All-Star weekend," Sue Bird said on the August 7 episode of her podcast, Bird's Eye View.

"The Lynx have already started to prove and show that they're the team to beat. They're a championship team. They were winning without her. So now it's just a matter of time to find that rhythm for Phee, for the team, for Phee and Olivia [Miles]."

While Napheesa Collier was sidelined, rookie Olivia Miles immediately stepped into a major role and helped the Lynx win 21 of their first 27 games. Miles, who is currently averaging 19.8 points, 4.8 rebounds and 5.8 assists, got support from veterans Kayla McBride, Natasha Howard and Courtney Williams, who also played key roles in keeping Minnesota at the top of the standings.

Get the Essentially W Newsletter. Everyday front-court analysis and back-court drama — where the W takes center court.

So, with Collier back, a championship-level team has only become an even stronger version of itself. Napheesa Collier has played five games so far and has already helped Minnesota win four of them. She is averaging 18.8 points, 7.4 rebounds, and 3.8 assists as the Lynx improve to 25-7 this season.

Yet there is still one question hanging over the Lynx, and that's whether Collier will stay with the team after the season concludes.

Analysts and experts had already floated block trade scenarios featuring Collier ahead of the trade deadline on August 2. However, Collier signed a one-year supermax contract with the Lynx, which has led to analysts speculating whether she'll leave after the season.

ESPN's Alexa Philippou had touched on Collier's expiring contract when discussing the free agency implications on Sports Center on August 1. Meanwhile, The Athletic's Annie Costabile was even more convincing.

"She signed a one-year, supermax deal for 2026 after being cored by the Lynx, and in doing so, she signaled to some degree that she'd like to explore her options in free agency."

However, after not making any major moves ahead of the trade window closing, the Lynx have their sights set on a championship, and Napheesa Collier is also focused on that same goal.

"I'm so focused on, right now, with my injury and this year and winning a championship. That is what I'm doing, so getting back with our amazing staff, playing with our amazing players and just focused on this year and winning." Collier told ESPN in April 2026.

So while the speculation about what happens when her contract ends remains part of the discussion, fans will be keeping their eyes on her to see what the next chapter holds for her.

title: Cubs newly-acquired pitcher Kevin Gausman already has nothing but love for new teammates
description: Kevin Gausman's Cubs debut had a rocky start, but his praise for his new teammates afterward said everything about how it ended.
fullText:
Cubs newly-acquired pitcher Kevin Gausman already has nothing but love for new teammates appeared first on ClutchPoints. 

Kevin Gausman's first outing in a Cubs uniform did not start smoothly, but it did not take long for his new team to win him over. The right-hander earned the win in his Chicago debut Friday night, tossing seven strong innings in a 6-4 victory over the Kansas City Royals, and he made sure to credit the defense behind him for helping settle him in.

"I can't say enough about this defense. You notice it right away," Gausman told reporters post-game. "Guys are running all over the place, putting their body on the line. A lot of fun."

"Man, I can't say enough about this defense. You notice it right away. Guys are running all over the place, putting their body on the line. A lot of fun."

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Kevin Gausman hypes up the Cubs' defense 👏 pic.twitter.com/ZUzlxgwm16

— Marquee Sports Network (@WatchMarquee) August 8, 2026

Gausman admitted his outing did not begin the way he wanted, walking the leadoff man and giving up two hits and a run in a shaky first inning.

"It took me a little bit to kind of get going. I was too quick, too amped up, trying to pitch great the first couple batters of the game," Gausman said. "I kind of got to let the game come to you. It took me kind of getting hit in the ankle to wake up a little bit, but we got through it, and me and Carson got on the same page."

The ankle scare came on a first-inning line drive off the bat of Salvador Perez that struck Gausman directly. He stayed in the game after a visit from the trainer and some warm-up throws, and the moment appeared to settle him rather than rattle him. From there, Gausman retired 19 of the final 21 batters he faced, allowing just a solo home run over the rest of his outing.

"I got lucky. It hit me half on my shoe, half on my leg. I'll take that," Gausman said. "I'll put some tape on it, put some ice on it the next couple days. I'll be all right."

Catcher Carson Kelly, working with Gausman for the first time, came away impressed with how the outing unfolded.

"It seemed like he got stronger as he went," Kelly said. "He's nasty."

The win extended Chicago's winning streak to five games and gave the Cubs exactly what they hoped for when they acquired Gausman from the Blue Jays at the deadline, a veteran arm capable of anchoring the rotation down the stretch as the team pushes for the postseason.

title: White Sox broadcaster's Steven Kwan 'power' take ages poorly seconds later

title: New MotoGP contract 'great news' for economy
description: The newly-signed deal will see more money being spent in the county and beyond, says track boss.
fullText:
An extension to Silverstone's deal to continue hosting MotoGP is a boost to the local and national economy, the track's managing director has said.

MotoGP and Silverstone announced the news to keep the highest class of motorbike racing at the Northamptonshire venue until 2028 earlier this week.

The move came as the track prepares to host this year's British Grand Prix, with tens of thousands of fans expected to attend on Sunday.

"It's great news," said Silverstone boss Stuart Pringle. "MotoGP is enjoying a strong period at the moment and we hope to introduce more and more motorsport fans to see this spectacular racing."

Pringle described the new MotoGP contract as "very important" for generating money both in the county and beyond.

"There's a lot of money spent in the local economy... but there's an awful lot more generated for the UK economy... through the industry," he said.

The managing director continued the extended deal supported jobs in the county, including seasonal weekend roles, while the number of the circuit's full-time staff had also increased.

"Having international motorsport events at the circuit has built the motor sport industry around Silverstone," said Pringle.

He added ticket prices for MotoGP were "more accessible" than for the track's Formula 1 event.

"It's the friendliest atmosphere here - it is a genuinely collegiate and happy festival atmosphere all weekend," he said.

Away from the track, Northamptonshire Police said people living near the circuit could expect to see increased community patrols by officers during the weekend.

Neighbourhood policing Ch Insp Dave Wakeman said officers would provide a "visible and reassuring presence in local communities and at campsites where many fans will be staying".

"We want everyone to enjoy the event for the right reasons, so please travel safely, use official parking and transport options, and be considerate of local residents and businesses," he said.
